Chapter 4 Energy principles and virtual work

4.8 Reciprocity: Betti's and Maxwell's theorems

So far we have loaded every body with a single load. The bracket of two bars from the beginning of the chapter, fixed to the wall, carried a load at the joint \(C\), the hanging bar its own weight. We computed the displacement of the joint \(C\) under the load in several ways, from the changes of the lengths of the bars in section 4.4, with the minimum of the total potential energy in section 4.6 and with virtual forces in section 4.7. Structures, however, usually carry several loads at once, and the loads change. Besides the load, the wind pushes on the bracket, and a lorry drives across a bridge, now here, now there. Do we have to compute everything again for every new combination of loads? And is there any connection between what one load causes and what another load causes?

From history

Engineers had the same question when computing statically indeterminate structures for moving loads, such as a truck on a bridge. They helped themselves with influence lines, which show how a chosen quantity, for example the displacement of a chosen point, changes as the load travels over the structure (TIMO, PDF pp. 224 and 259). In drawing these lines a theorem came in handy that Maxwell presented in 1864 for the case of two forces (CM, PDF p. 320, TIMO, PDF p. 259, EP, p. 230). It says that the displacement of the second point in the direction of the second force, caused by the first force, equals the displacement of the first point in the direction of the first force, caused by the second force, if the forces are equally large. Why does this help? Take a beam on two supports with the points \(A\) and \(B\) on it. The downward displacement of the point \(A\) when the load stands at the point \(B\) equals the downward displacement of the point \(B\) when the same load stands at \(A\). To get the displacement of the point \(A\) for a load at every place \(B\), we therefore do not need to put the load at every place separately. One load at \(A\) and the displacements of all points \(B\) are enough.

The general proof was given in 1872 by Enrico Betti, so one says that Betti generalized Maxwell's work (EP, p. 230, CM, PDF p. 320, TIMO, PDF p. 259-260). John William Strutt, Lord Rayleigh, extended it to the vibration of elastic systems (TIMO, PDF p. 259-260, LOVE, PDF p. 192).

The goal of the section is three results that answer both questions from the beginning of the section. They hold for bodies of a linear elastic material with small displacements. The first says that the effects of loads add up: the displacements and stresses caused by two loads together are the sum of the displacements and stresses that each causes alone. The second compares the work of two loads. The work that the first load would do on the displacements caused by the second equals the work that the second load would do on the displacements caused by the first. The third is a special case of the second for two forces, each of magnitude 1 N. The displacement of the point of application of the first force in its direction, caused by the second force, equals the displacement of the point of application of the second force in its direction, caused by the first force. The second result is named after Betti (1823-1892), the third after Maxwell (1831-1879) (EP §4.6.4 and §4.6.5, pp. 227 and 230). The property that the roles of two loads may be exchanged is called reciprocity (vzajemnost).

The route is as follows. First we compute the displacement of the joint \(C\) of the bracket under an arbitrary force at the joint. In the result we notice both phenomena: the displacement is a sum of contributions of the two components of the force, and the horizontal displacement caused by a vertical force equals the vertical displacement caused by an equally large horizontal force. We prove the first phenomenon for every body. The second we first explain with the work the two forces do when we put them on the bracket in different orders, and then we prove it for every body, from the principle of virtual displacements and the symmetry of the elastic constants. At the end we obtain the third result from it, test it on the bracket and on the hanging bar, and show how it is used in measurement.

The physical model is the same as in section 4.6. Let us list the assumptions and say for each where we use it.

  1. Small displacements. The strains are small. Equilibrium and strains are computed on the shape of the body before loading, the strain with the small strain tensor (definition 1.121). In the bracket the strains of the bars are smaller than one thousandth (section 4.1.4). Therefore all equations that determine the displacements are linear, which we use when adding loads, and the principle of virtual displacements holds (theorem 4.82), on which the proofs of both theorems of the section rest.
  2. Linear and ideal elastic material. The stresses are below the yield stress, as in the steel bars of the bracket (section 4.1.4). The stress components are linear functions of the strain components, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\) (definition 3.25), and the material stores the work it receives and returns it on unloading (definition 3.58). Therefore \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) (theorem 3.62 on the symmetry of the elastic constants). We use the linearity when adding loads and the symmetry of the constants in the proof of the relation between the works of two loads.
  3. Stable material. The strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero (section 3.6.9). We use it when we show that a load determines the displacements uniquely.
  4. Loads independent of the deformation. The magnitude and direction of the loads do not change with the deformation (section 4.6.3). Therefore the work of a load on displacements is the work of a constant force, as in Clapeyron's theorem.
  5. Fixed supports. On a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface the body is held, and the displacement there is zero, for all the loads we compare. The supports shall prevent every small rigid displacement of the body, that is, a translation and a small rotation of the body as a whole, in which the distances between its points do not change. We use the first in both theorems, the second for uniqueness.
  6. Slow loading. The forces grow so slowly that the velocities of the points are negligible, as in section 4.1. We need it only in the explanation with the order of loading. The proofs do not need it, because they speak only about final states.

4.8.1 The bracket with two forces

The bracket is the one from section 4.1.4, with the same axes, dimensions and material (figure 4.409, left). The axis \(x\) points horizontally to the right, the axis \(y\) vertically up, and the origin is at the joint \(C\). The horizontal bar \(AC\) has the length \(L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 4\) m, the inclined bar \(BC\) the length \(L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 5\) m. The pin \(A\) and the pin \(B\), which is 3 m above it, are fixed to the wall. For both steel bars \(EA = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N, from \(E = 196\) GPa and the cross-sectional area \(10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2\). The truss model (definition 4.4) and the assumption that a compressed bar stays straight, without buckling, remain. The only new thing is that instead of the load an arbitrary force in the plane of the bracket acts at the joint \(C\), \(\vek F = (F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\). The load from the beginning of the chapter is the case \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -10\) kN.

We denote the displacement of the joint \(C\) by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = (u, v, 0)\), as in sections 4.4.9 and 4.6.5: \(u\) is the horizontal displacement, positive to the right, \(v\) the vertical displacement, positive upwards. Let us compute them in five steps.

  1. Equilibrium of the pin \(C\). We cut the pin out (figure 4.409, middle). On it act the components of the force and the two bars. A bar with the axial force \(N\) acts on the pin with the force \(-N\,\vek n\), where \(\vek n\) is the unit vector along the bar from the wall towards \(C\), \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}} = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0)\) (section 4.1.4). A bar in tension therefore pulls the pin towards the wall, the bar \(AC\) horizontally to the left, the bar \(BC\) obliquely towards the pin \(B\), 4 units to the left for every 3 units up. We took the directions of the bars from the shape before loading (assumption 1). May we? Under the load of 10 kN the end of the bar \(BC\) moves across the bar by 10,2 mm, which we compute from the displacement checked below. The bar, 5 m long, therefore turns by \(10{,}2\ \text{mm}/5000\ \text{mm} = 0{,}002\) radians, and the two forces turn by as much, so the result changes by a few thousandths. For displacements comparable with the length of the bars we would have to write the equilibrium on the displaced shape, and the equations would no longer be linear. The sum of the three forces on the pin is zero:
    \[(F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0) - N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,(1, 0, 0) - N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\tfrac15\,(4, -3, 0) = (0, 0, 0) .\]
  2. The forces in the bars. Besides the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), only the force of the inclined bar has a vertical component, namely three fifths of its magnitude. The \(y\) component of the equation therefore gives \(F_{\mathrm{y}} + \tfrac35\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\). In the horizontal direction act the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), the force of the bar \(AC\) and four fifths of the force of the bar \(BC\). The \(x\) component gives \(F_{\mathrm{x}} - N_{\mathrm{AC}} - \tfrac45\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), so \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = F_{\mathrm{x}} - \tfrac45\,N_{\mathrm{BC}} = F_{\mathrm{x}} + \tfrac43\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\). For the load, \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -10\) kN, we get \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}67\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}33\) kN, as in section 4.1.4.
  3. The elongations of the bars. A bar with a constant axial force \(N\) gets longer by \(\Delta L = N L/(EA)\) (section 4.1.4). For our two bars, 4 m and 5 m long, \(L_{\mathrm{AC}}/(EA) = 4\ \text{m}/(EA)\) and \(L_{\mathrm{BC}}/(EA) = 5\ \text{m}/(EA)\), so
    \[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = \frac{4\ \text{m}}{EA}\,\Big(F_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac43\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\Big) , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \frac{5\ \text{m}}{EA}\,\Big({-\frac53}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\Big) .\]
  4. The elongations from the displacement. The joint moves from \(C\) to \(C_1\), by \(u\) to the right and by \(v\) up (figure 4.409, right, where only the ends of the bars at the joint are drawn and the displacement is strongly enlarged). For small displacements the change of length of a bar is the projection of the displacement of the joint \(C\) onto the direction of the bar. We showed this for a virtual displacement in equation (4.49), and since the derivation used only that the displacement is small, in section 4.4.9 we used the same for the actual displacement, \(\Delta L = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\). For the bar \(AC\) we project the displacement onto the horizontal direction and get simply \(u\). For the bar \(BC\) we project it onto the continuation of the bar beyond the joint: we drop a perpendicular from \(C_1\) onto it, and the distance from \(C\) to its foot is \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}\). A displacement to the right makes the bar \(BC\) longer, a displacement upwards makes it shorter, so
    \[\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u , \qquad \Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac45\,u - \tfrac35\,v .\]
    What did the projection neglect? The part of the displacement perpendicular to the bar. It mostly turns the bar. By the Pythagorean theorem the length of the bar after the displacement is \(\sqrt{(L + a)^2 + b^2} \approx L + a + b^2/(2L)\), where \(a\) is the part of the displacement along the bar and \(b\) the part perpendicular to it, so we neglected \(b^2/(2L)\). Under the load of 10 kN this is, for the bar \(BC\), \((10{,}2\ \text{mm})^2/(2 \cdot 5000\ \text{mm}) = 0{,}010\) mm against the elongation of \(4{,}252\) mm, that is two and a half thousandths. The neglected part grows with the square of the displacement and the elongation only with its first power, so for a load twice as large this share is twice as large.
  5. The displacement. From the first equation of step 4, \(u = \Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}\), from the second \(v = \tfrac43\,u - \tfrac53\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}\). We insert the elongations from step 3:
    \[u = \frac{4\ \text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{16}{3}\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad v = \frac{16}{3}\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + 21\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} . \tag{4.88}\]
    Where do the numbers come from? The number \(\tfrac{16}{3}\) in the expression for \(u\) is \(4 \cdot \tfrac43\) from the elongation of the bar \(AC\), and in the expression for \(v\) it is \(\tfrac43 \cdot 4\) from the term \(\tfrac43\,u\). The number 21 is the sum of the contributions of the two bars:
    \[21 = \underbrace{\frac43 \cdot \frac{16}{3}}_{\text{bar } \mathrm{AC}} + \underbrace{\frac53 \cdot 5 \cdot \frac53}_{\text{bar } \mathrm{BC}} = \frac{64}{9} + \frac{125}{9} .\]
    We have already drawn both parts of the number 21. For the load of 10 kN they are 3,628 mm, by which the shortening of the bar \(AC\) lowers the joint, and 7,086 mm, by which the elongation of the bar \(BC\) lowers it (figure 4.297).

Let us check with the load. For \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -10^4\) N

\[u = \frac{16}{3} \cdot \frac{1\ \text{m} \cdot (-10^4\ \text{N})}{1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\ \text{N}} = -2{,}721\ \text{mm} , \qquad v = 21 \cdot \frac{1\ \text{m} \cdot (-10^4\ \text{N})}{1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\ \text{N}} = -10{,}71\ \text{mm} .\]

Under the load the joint moves by 2,721 mm towards the wall and by 10,71 mm down (figure 4.297, right), as we computed in sections 4.4, 4.6 and 4.7. The horizontal displacement is exactly the shortening of the compressed bar \(AC\), because this bar is horizontal.

The result (4.88) shows two things. The first is that each component of the displacement is a sum of two terms, one proportional to \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the other proportional to \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\). The force \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) therefore causes the sum of the displacements that the forces \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\) and \((0, F_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\) would cause each alone, and a force twice as large causes a displacement twice as large. Why? In each of the five steps we only multiplied numbers by constant numbers and added them. We wrote the equilibrium on the shape before loading, so the directions \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\) do not depend on the force. The elongation of a bar is proportional to its force, and the projection is a sum of products of components with constant numbers.

Let us name the four numbers in front of the forces in (4.88):

\[u = D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad v = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} + D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} .\]

The first index gives the direction of the displacement, the second the direction of the force. Each number is a displacement per newton of force. The number \(D_{\mathrm{yx}}\), for example, is the vertical displacement of the joint caused by a horizontal force of 1 N. For our bracket

\[\begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{4\ \text{m}}{EA} = 204{,}1\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} , \\ D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}} &= \frac{16}{3}\,\frac{\text{m}}{EA} = 272{,}1\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} , \\ D_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \frac{21\ \text{m}}{EA} = 1071{,}4\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} , \end{aligned}\]

where we wrote the displacements in micrometres per kilonewton of force. The second thing the result shows is exactly the equality \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\). A horizontal force of 1 kN to the right moves the joint by 272,1 µm up, and a vertical force of 1 kN upwards moves it by 272,1 µm to the right (figure 4.410). The same figure shows the other two displacements, \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot D_{\mathrm{xx}} = 204{,}1\) µm to the right for the horizontal force and \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot D_{\mathrm{yy}} = 1071{,}4\) µm up for the vertical one.

Let us look at how each of the two displacements arises. The pins \(A\) and \(B\) are on the wall and do not move, so the joint \(C\) can be moved only by a change of length of the bars and their turning about the pins. For the horizontal force \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN, step 2 gives the forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\). The bar \(AC\) gets longer by \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot D_{\mathrm{xx}} = 204{,}1\) µm, while the bar \(BC\) keeps its length. The joint \(C\) must therefore stay 5 m from the pin \(B\) and moves to the position \(C_1\) along the circle about \(B\), for a small displacement perpendicular to the bar \(BC\) (figure 4.410, left). The second equation of step 4 with \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) gives \(v = \tfrac43\,u = \tfrac43 \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = 272{,}1\) µm. Here the factor \(\tfrac43\) comes from geometry: the direction perpendicular to the bar \(BC\) goes 4 units up for every 3 units sideways. We made the same argument in section 4.7 for the displacement under the load (figure 4.297). For the vertical force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN upwards, step 2 gives the forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac43\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) kN. The joint moves from \(C\) to \(C_1\). The horizontal displacement is the elongation of the bar \(AC\), \(\tfrac43\ \text{kN} \cdot 4\ \text{m}/(EA) = 272{,}1\) µm (figure 4.410, right). Here the factor \(\tfrac43\) comes from equilibrium: this many kilonewtons must be carried by the horizontal bar when the inclined bar balances the vertical force of 1 kN. The same triangle with the sides 3, 4 and 5, two different routes, the same number. Is this a coincidence of this bracket? It is not. In the next two subsections we will see that the equality holds for every elastic body, and that its reason is the work the two forces do.

4.8.2 Adding loads

The first observation holds for every body that satisfies the assumptions from the beginning of the section. To state it precisely, we must first say which displacement field the body takes under a given load. Let the body be as in theorem 4.82 on the principle of virtual displacements (figure 4.226): before loading it occupies the set of points \(V\) with the surface \(S\). On a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of the surface it is held, and on the remaining part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) a prescribed traction vector \(\bar{\vek t}\) acts on it, the force per unit area with which the surroundings act on the body. A body force \(\vek b\) acts in the body (definition 2.28). The displacement field that the body takes in equilibrium must meet three requirements, which combine what we learned in the first three chapters: strains from displacements, the relation between stresses and strains, and equilibrium.

Definition 4.133 Solution for a load (rešitev za obremenitev)

Let the body \(V\) and the division of its surface into the parts \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) be as in theorem 4.82 on the principle of virtual displacements, and let the displacement \(\vek 0\) be prescribed on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). Let the material be linear elastic, with the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}\) (definition 3.25). A load on the body is a pair \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\): a body force \(\vek b\), continuous on \(V\), and a prescribed traction vector \(\bar{\vek t}\), continuous on each outer face of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). A displacement field \(\vek u\) is a solution for the load \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\) if:

  1. \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable (definition 1.91) on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, and is equal to \(\vek 0\) at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\),
  2. the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\), computed from the components \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek u\), are continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body together with its surface, and satisfy the equilibrium equations (2.38) at every interior point of the body,
  3. Cauchy's formula \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) holds at every point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), where \(\vek n\) is the outward unit normal of the surface.

Source: EP §4.6.1, (4.6.1)-(4.6.4) (p. 218), SADD §6.2 (PDF p. 133), BOWER §5.8.1 (PDF p. 379).

The first requirement says that the field respects the supports and has a small strain tensor at every point. The second says that the stresses are as the material requires, and that every small piece of the body, also with the body force that acts on it, is in equilibrium (theorem 2.31). The third says that the stresses at the surface carry the prescribed forces. All three requirements are written on the shape of the body before loading, as assumption 1 requires.

Let us look on a bar at what the requirements distinguish (figure 4.411).

Take a steel bar with the modulus \(E = 196\) GPa, cross-section area \(A = 100\) mm\(^2\) and length \(L = 1\) m, fixed at \(x = 0\) and loaded at the end \(x = L\) with the force \(F = 10\) kN, so with the prescribed stress \(\bar t = F/A = 100\) MPa. We describe it with the model of section 4.1, in which every cross section moves only along the axis by \(u(x)\) and the stress is \(\sigma = E\,u'\). There is no body force. The field \(u = \varepsilon x\) with \(\varepsilon = F/(EA) = 10\,000\ \text{N}/(196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2) = 5{,}102 \cdot 10^{-4}\) is a solution. Let us check the requirements on the top bar of the figure. At \(x = 0\) we have \(u = 0\) (requirement 1), and the end moves by \(\varepsilon L = 0{,}5102\) mm. The stress \(\sigma = E\varepsilon = 100\) MPa is constant, so the equilibrium equation \(\mathrm{d}\sigma/\mathrm{d}x = 0\) holds (requirement 2). We see what this means if in thought we cut an inner piece out of the bar: on both cuts the rest of the bar pulls it with the force \(\sigma A = 10\) kN, the two forces are opposite and the piece stays at rest. Requirement 3 is the same equilibrium for a thin slice at the end of the bar. From the left the bar pulls it with the force \(\sigma A = 10\) kN, from the right the prescribed force \(\bar t A = 10\) kN. The forces are equal, \(\sigma = \bar t\), and the slice stays at rest.

The field \(u = 1{,}01\,\varepsilon x\) differs from the solution by one percent (the bottom bar of figure 4.411, which is pulled by the force \(F = 10\) kN as well). It is continuously differentiable and zero at \(x = 0\) (requirement 1), while the end moves by \(0{,}5153\) mm, \(5{,}1\) µm more. The stress \(\sigma = 1{,}01 \cdot 100 = 101\) MPa is constant, so the equilibrium equation holds (requirement 2): the inner piece is pulled by the forces \(10{,}1\) kN to the left and \(10{,}1\) kN to the right, and the piece stays at rest. But requirement 3 does not hold. The end slice is pulled to the left by the bar with the force \(\sigma A = 10{,}1\) kN, while the prescribed force to the right is only \(10\) kN, since \(\sigma = 101\) MPa \(\neq 100\) MPa \(= \bar t\). There remain \(0{,}1\) kN to the left that nothing balances, and the slice would not stay at rest. The field respects the support and is in equilibrium in the interior, and yet it is not a solution: only requirement 3 rejects it.

The stresses of a solution are symmetric, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{ji}}\), because the elastic constants are symmetric in the first pair of indices, \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}}\) (lemma 3.26, item 2). A solution therefore satisfies the assumptions that the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.82) makes about the stresses, and, if its strains are small, the assumptions that the principle of minimum total potential energy (theorem 4.91) makes about the true displacement field. Can one load have two different solutions? Let us draw what that would mean (figure 4.412, top).

The body is glued to the wall with its left face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), and the prescribed load \(\bar{\vek t}\) acts on the right face. Suppose the same load could bring it into the shape given by the field \(\vek u\), or into another shape given by the field \(\tilde{\vek u}\). The difference \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) says by how much the two shapes differ at each point. Then we could not speak of the displacement that the load causes, because there would be two of them.

This does not happen, and the reason is energy (the middle row of figure 4.412). On the horizontal axis we mark the fields \(\vek u + s\,\vek v\) for the numbers \(s\) from \(0\) to \(1\), which lead from \(\vek u\) to \(\tilde{\vek u}\), and on the vertical axis their total potential energy \(\Pi\). If \(\vek u\) is a solution, then by the principle of minimum total potential energy (theorem 4.91) the energy of every other admissible field is larger by the strain energy of the difference of the fields. For the field \(\vek u + s\,\vek v\) the difference is \(s\,\vek v\). Its strain energy is \(s^2\,U(\vek v)\), because the strain energy density is a sum of products of two strain components each (lemma 4.90) and every component carries the factor \(s\). The energy is therefore a parabola with its lowest point at \(\vek u\), and \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u})\) lies \(U(\vek v)\) above \(\Pi(\vek u)\). But \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is a solution too, and the same conclusion gives a parabola with its lowest point at \(\tilde{\vek u}\), on which \(\Pi(\vek u)\) lies \(U(\vek v)\) above \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u})\). Each of two energies cannot be higher than the other. Both pictures hold at once only if \(U(\vek v) = 0\) and the line is horizontal. But the strain energy is zero only for a field without strain, and such a field is a rigid displacement. The lemma says this precisely.

Lemma 4.134 Uniqueness of the solution (enoličnost rešitve)

Let the body be as in definition 4.133, of a homogeneous (definition 3.11) and ideal elastic material whose strain energy density is positive for every small strain that is not zero. Let the body be in one piece: its interior points form a connected open set (definition 1.136), and every point of the body is the limit of a sequence of its interior points, so that the body has no parts without an interior, such as a sheet without thickness. Let \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) be solutions for the same load \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\), both with small strains. Then:

  1. the strains and stresses of the two solutions are equal at every point of the body,
  2. the difference \(\tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is a small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\). If the supports prevent every small rigid displacement of the body, then \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\).
Proof

We must show that the difference of the two solutions has no strain, and draw from this the conclusions about the stresses and the displacements. We use the principle of minimum total potential energy, once for each solution (first, then).

  1. By requirement 1 of definition 4.133 both fields are continuously differentiable and equal to \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so they are kinematically admissible displacement fields with the prescribed displacement \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) (definition 4.88).
  2. By requirements 2 and 3 the stresses of the field \(\vek u\) are continuously differentiable and satisfy the equilibrium equations and, on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), Cauchy's formula, and they are symmetric because \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}}\) (lemma 3.26, item 2). The material is homogeneous, ideal and linear elastic with a positive strain energy density, both fields have small strains, and the load \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t})\) is given and does not change with the deformation, as the theorem requires. By theorem 4.91 on the principle of minimum total potential energy, item 1, applied with the other admissible field \(\tilde{\vek u}\), therefore \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) - \Pi(\vek u) \ge 0\).
  3. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is a solution too, so we may exchange the roles, and the same theorem gives \(\Pi(\vek u) - \Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) \ge 0\).
  4. A number that is not negative and whose opposite is not negative either is zero, so \(\Pi(\tilde{\vek u}) = \Pi(\vek u)\). By item 2 of the same theorem the small strain tensor of the field \(\vek v = \tilde{\vek u} - \vek u\) is zero at every point of the body.
  5. A partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives (lemma 1.82), so the strain of the field \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u + \vek v\) is the sum of the strains of the fields \(\vek u\) and \(\vek v\), and thus equal to the strain of the field \(\vek u\). The stresses are computed from the strains (definition 3.25), so they are equal too. This is item 1.
  1. The field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable on the intersection of the two open sets of requirement 1, which is again an open set that contains the body together with its surface, since the fields \(\vek u\) and \(\tilde{\vek u}\) are continuously differentiable there (lemma 1.82, corollary 1.70, item 1). By step 4 it has a zero small strain tensor at every point of the body. The interior points of the body form a connected open set. So by theorem 1.140 on a displacement field without strain there are a constant vector \(\vek a\) and a constant antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\) such that \(\vek v(P) = \vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) at every interior point \(P\). Figure 4.413 draws the case \(\vek a = \vek 0\), a rotation about the point \(O\): at every point the displacement arrow is perpendicular to the line to \(O\), and the farther the point is from \(O\), the longer the arrow. A continuously differentiable field is continuous (section 1.15.6), and the field \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) is a polynomial in the coordinates and therefore continuous (corollary 1.70, item 2). Let \(P\) be a point of the surface and \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) a sequence of interior points that converges to \(P\): every circle about \(P\), however small, contains all terms from some term on. By lemma 1.69, used for each component, the sequence \(\vek v(P_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(\vek v(P)\), and the sequence \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP_{\mathrm{n}}}\) to \(\vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\). The two sequences are equal term by term, so by lemma 1.42 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence their limits are equal too, and the equality holds at the points of the surface as well. By (2.39), \(\mat W\,\vek r = \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\vek r\) for \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = (W_{\mathrm{zy}}, W_{\mathrm{xz}}, W_{\mathrm{yx}})\), which we check component by component, for the component \(x\) for example \(W_{\mathrm{xx}}\,x + W_{\mathrm{xy}}\,y + W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z = W_{\mathrm{xz}}\,z - W_{\mathrm{yx}}\,y\), because \(W_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) (lemma 1.104, item 3) and \(W_{\mathrm{xy}} = -W_{\mathrm{yx}}\). So the field \(\vek v\) is a small rigid displacement of lemma 4.72 with \(\delta\vek a = \vek a\), like the rotation of the bar about the point \(O\). On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(\vek v = \vek 0 - \vek 0 = \vek 0\).
  2. If the supports prevent every small rigid displacement, as a face glued to the wall prevents it, the only small rigid displacement that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the field \(\vek 0\). Therefore \(\vek v = \vek 0\) and \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\). This is item 2.

Source: SADD §6.2, (6.2.1)-(6.2.5) (PDF p. 133), EP §4.6.3, (4.6.14)-(4.6.21) (pp. 225-226), CM (7.3.45) (PDF p. 314). The sources insert the difference of the two solutions directly into the strain energy. The proof with the principle of minimum total potential energy is not from the sources. The statement in step 6, that a field without strain is a small rigid displacement, SADD states without proof (PDF p. 133), and in this book it is proved by theorem 1.140 on a displacement field without strain.

The proof showed why there is only one solution: the difference of two solutions has no strain and can only be a rigid displacement, which the supports do not allow. What if they allow it (the bottom row of figure 4.412)? The hanging bar of chapter 1 is held only at the centre \(O\) of its top face. A fixed point prevents a translation, but not a rotation of the bar about \(O\), in which the lower end moves sideways while the distances between the points of the bar stay the same. So CM adds the condition that the material at the point \(O\) does not rotate (CM, PDF p. 306). Without this condition the stresses would still be determined uniquely, the displacements only up to a small rotation. A body glued to the wall with the whole face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) cannot undergo such a rotation. If we rotate it about the lower edge of the face, the upper edge of the face moves away from its place, but the displacement on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) must be zero. In the wall bracket of two bars the pins \(A\) and \(B\) are enough. The two elongations determined the displacement of the joint \(C\) uniquely in steps 4 and 5 of subsection 4.8.1: \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u\) and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac45\,u - \tfrac35\,v\) give \(u\) and \(v\) uniquely, since the two bars are not parallel.

Let us also look at where the proof uses the assumptions of the lemma. The positive strain energy density and the homogeneity are used in step 4, through item 2 of the theorem. For a stable material such as steel it holds, because every deformation takes work (section 3.6.9). A material that deformed without energy under some strain would have a horizontal line also for a difference \(\vek v\) with that strain, and the load would not determine even the strains. The theorem needs the homogeneity so that the energy density of the difference is a continuous function of the point. For a piece glued together from two materials the elastic constants jump at the interface, and the proof of the theorem would have to be repeated on each part separately. Step 6 uses the two assumptions on a body in one piece. Without the first, theorem 1.140 on a displacement field without strain fails, as the two separate cubes of figure 1.469 show, each of which moves rigidly in its own way: the left one stays, the right one moves by \(\vek a\). The second carries the equality \(\vek v = \vek a + \mat W\,\overrightarrow{OP}\) from the interior points to the surface, where the supports are. Only because of it does the condition \(\vek v = \vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) restrict the rigid displacement. The point \(Q\) on a sheet without thickness attached to the body does not satisfy this assumption: a small circle about it contains no interior point of the body, so the equality cannot be carried to it. For a body made of boxes the second assumption holds by itself, as we saw in step 3 of the proof of theorem 4.82.

Now we can state the first observation for every body. Let us first look at it on the bar of the example from the beginning of the subsection (figure 4.414, left).

The force \(10\) kN gives in the bar, fixed to the wall, the stress \(100\) MPa and moves the end by \(0{,}5102\) mm. The force \(5\) kN gives in the same bar the stress \(50\) MPa and the end displacement \(0{,}2551\) mm. Let us apply both at once, together \(15\) kN. The stress is \(150\) MPa \(= 100\) MPa \(+ 50\) MPa, and the end displacement \(0{,}7653\) mm \(= 0{,}5102\) mm \(+ 0{,}2551\) mm. The lemma says that this holds for every body. Its proof goes up the same steps as the computation for the bar: the displacements add, so the strains do, so the stresses do, and these carry the sum of the loads.

Lemma 4.135 Principle of superposition (načelo superpozicije)

Let the body be as in definition 4.133, let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\), with the strains \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the stresses \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be numbers. Then the field \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) is a solution for the load

\[\big(\alpha\,\vek b^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek b^{(2)},\ \alpha\,\bar{\vek t}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\big) ,\]

its strains are \(\alpha\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and its stresses \(\alpha\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Proof

For the field \(\vek u = \alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) we must check the three requirements of definition 4.133. Each follows from the requirement being linear.

  1. A partial derivative of a sum is the sum of the partial derivatives, and a partial derivative of a multiple is the multiple of the partial derivative (lemma 1.82). A sum of continuous functions of a point and a multiple of a continuous function are continuous functions (corollary 1.70, item 1). Therefore \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable on the intersection of the two open sets of requirement 1, which is again an open set that contains the body together with its surface. On \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), for the bar at the wall, \(\vek u = \alpha\,\vek 0 + \beta\,\vek 0 = \vek 0\). This is requirement 1.
  2. By the same rule for derivatives, \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \alpha\,\partial u^{(1)}_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \beta\,\partial u^{(2)}_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\) and \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\). The component of the small strain tensor \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{j}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}})\) is therefore \(\alpha\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\), as for the bar the two elongations add.
  3. By definition 3.25 the stresses are
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\big(\alpha\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}} + \beta\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\big) = \alpha \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}} + \beta \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}} = \alpha\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} ,\]
    because a finite sum may be split into two sums and the constant numbers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) taken out. For the bar this is \(150 = 100 + 50\) MPa. By step 1, applied to the stresses, they are continuously differentiable.
  4. We insert the stresses from step 3 and the body force \(\alpha\,\vek b^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek b^{(2)}\) into the first equilibrium equation (2.38) and use the rule for derivatives from step 1:
    \[\frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} = \alpha\,\Big(\frac{\partial\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b^{(1)}_{\mathrm{x}}\Big) + \beta\,\Big(\frac{\partial\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b^{(2)}_{\mathrm{x}}\Big) .\]
    Both brackets are zero, because \(\vek u^{(1)}\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) are solutions, so the left side is \(\alpha \cdot 0 + \beta \cdot 0 = 0\). The same holds for the second and third equilibrium equations. This is requirement 2.
  5. On \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the component \(i\) of the column \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is, by (1.39),
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \big(\alpha\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} + \beta\,\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\big)\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \alpha \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} + \beta \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} ,\]
    where we split the finite sum and took out the numbers as in step 3. On the right are the components \(i\) of the columns \(\ten\sigma^{(1)}\vek n = \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\) and \(\ten\sigma^{(2)}\vek n = \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\), so \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \alpha\,\bar{\vek t}^{(1)} + \beta\,\bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\), as at the end of the bar, which carries \(15 = 10 + 5\) kN. This is requirement 3.

Source: EP §4.6.1, (4.6.1)-(4.6.4) (pp. 217-218), CM §7.4.1 (PDF p. 314). EP states the principle for all problems that are linear geometrically and in the material, but does not write a proof. The proof in steps is not from the sources.

The lemma together with lemma 4.134 on the uniqueness of the solution says what we saw in the computation for the bracket. If the supports prevent rigid displacements and \(\alpha\,\vek u^{(1)} + \beta\,\vek u^{(2)}\) has small strains, it is the only solution with small strains for the combined load. We may therefore compute the displacements and stresses of two loads separately and add them, and a load increased by the factor \(\alpha\) causes \(\alpha\) times larger displacements and stresses. This holds as long as the material is linear elastic. The bar with the force \(10\) kN and the stress \(100\) MPa reaches the yield stress \(220\) MPa at the factor \(\alpha = 220/100 = 2{,}2\), and above it adding fails, as we show below. It is therefore enough to compute the effect of each load on a structure once, and the combinations follow by adding. The same holds for the bracket, which is not a body in the sense of the definition but a model of bars. There the linearity was shown by the computation (4.88), and on the right side of figure 4.414 we see it. In the plane with the axes \(u\) and \(v\) in micrometres let us draw the displacements of the joint \(C\). The force \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN moves it by \(\vek u^{(1)} = (204{,}1,\ 272{,}1)\) µm, the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN by \(\vek u^{(2)} = (272{,}1,\ 1071{,}4)\) µm, as in figure 4.410. Under both forces at once the joint comes to the point \((476{,}2,\ 1343{,}5)\) µm, the opposite corner of the parallelogram spanned by the two displacements: \(204{,}1 + 272{,}1 = 476{,}2\) and \(272{,}1 + 1071{,}4 = 1343{,}5\).

When does adding fail? Each of the linearities we used can fail (figure 4.416).

The first is the assumption of small displacements, by which we write the equilibrium on the shape before loading. For the bracket it is justified (figure 4.415). The bracket with bars \(4\) m and \(5\) m long, pinned to the wall at \(A\) and \(B\), goes under the load \(10\) kN into a new shape. The joint \(C\) drops by \(10{,}71\) mm and moves \(2{,}72\) mm to the left. So the bar \(AC\) turns by \(10{,}71\ \text{mm}/4000\ \text{mm} = 0{,}0027\) radians, the bar \(BC\) by \(0{,}0020\) radians, both by less than three thousandths of a radian. The directions in which the two bars act on the joint change by the same angles, so the equilibrium equations of the joint hardly change. Equilibrium on the displaced shape gives \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = -13{,}32\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 16{,}68\) kN instead of \(-13{,}33\) kN and \(16{,}67\) kN, the forces change by less than one thousandth.

But where it is the change of shape itself that carries the load, the assumption fails. Take a steel wire with the cross section \(1\) mm\(^2\), so with \(EA = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^5\) N, stretched straight and without force between two walls that are \(2a = 2\) m apart, and load it at the middle with the force \(F = 5\) N perpendicular to the wire. The force in a wire points along the wire, so a straight wire cannot carry a transverse force. The middle sags by \(\delta\), and only the inclined halves of the wire carry the force. So we must write the equilibrium on the shape after loading. Let us compute the sag in three steps.

  1. Elongation. By the Pythagorean theorem each half of the wire is \(\sqrt{a^2 + \delta^2}\) long. Since \(\big(a + \delta^2/(2a)\big)^2 = a^2 + \delta^2 + \delta^4/(4a^2)\), this is approximately \(a + \delta^2/(2a)\) for small \(\delta/a\). The strain of the wire is therefore \(\varepsilon = \delta^2/(2a^2)\) and the force in it \(N = EA\,\delta^2/(2a^2)\).
  2. Equilibrium of the middle. A half of the wire descends by \(\delta\) over the length \(a\), so the vertical component of its force is approximately \(N\,\delta/a\). The two halves together carry the force, \(F = 2N\,\delta/a\).
  3. Sag. We insert \(N\) from step 1:
    \[F = EA\,\Big(\frac{\delta}{a}\Big)^3 , \qquad \delta = a\,\sqrt[3]{\frac{F}{EA}} .\]

For \(F = 5\) N, \(\delta = 1\ \text{m} \cdot \sqrt[3]{5/(1{,}96 \cdot 10^5)} = 29{,}44\) mm. The computation without the approximations of steps 1 and 2, done numerically, gives \(29{,}44\) mm, so to four digits the approximations change nothing. Let us double the force to \(10\) N. If the effects added, the wire would sag by \(2 \cdot 29{,}44 = 58{,}9\) mm. It sags only by \(37{,}09\) mm (\(37{,}10\) mm without the approximations), \(\sqrt[3]{2} = 1{,}26\) times as much. On the graph of the force against the sag both computed sags lie on a curve of the third degree. Adding would require a straight line through the origin, along which twice the force would give twice the sag. A straight line through the origin is the picture of the principle of superposition: twice as high means twice as far.

The second linearity is the law of the material. A material above the yield stress (definition 2.7) or rubber at large stretches is not linear elastic. Idealized steel follows a straight line up to the yield stress \(220\) MPa, and above it the stress no longer grows. The bar from the left of figure 4.414 has under the force \(10\) kN the stress \(100\) MPa and the strain \(0{,}000510\), and under the force \(15\) kN the stress \(150\) MPa. Adding would give the stress \(250\) MPa under both forces at once, \(25\) kN. Idealized steel does not reach it: the bar carries at most \(220\ \text{MPa} \cdot 100\ \text{mm}^2 = 22\) kN and cannot balance the force \(25\) kN. The third is a load independent of the deformation. A load that changes with the deformation does not allow adding. Such is water pressure on a plate that tilts (section 4.6.3). The force of the water is perpendicular to the plate and turns with it. If a second load tilts the plate further, the force of the water under both loads at once is turned by another angle than under the water alone, so the sum of the two solutions does not carry the true force of the water. At a tilt of \(0{,}01\) radians the force gets a transverse component of almost exactly \(1\) % of its magnitude, since \(\sin 0{,}01 = 0{,}0099998\). The fourth is supports that are the same for all loads. Adding fails for a support that can only push the body and cannot pull it. A board that lies on a table is pressed against the table by a force downwards along its whole length. A force upwards at the end lifts the board off the table there, and the part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) on which the displacement is zero is shorter. But definition 4.133 requires the same part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) for both loads.

Displacements and stresses add up, but energy does not. Take the bracket with a horizontal force \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN and a vertical force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN upwards at the joint \(C\). By step 2 of subsection 4.8.1 the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) alone gives the axial forces \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\), the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) alone \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac43\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) kN, and both together the sums, \(N_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac73\) kN and \(N_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) kN. The strain energy of the bracket is \(U = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}^2 L_{\mathrm{i}}/(2EA)\) by (4.5), and with SymPy we get

\[U(F_{\mathrm{x}}) = 0{,}1020\ \text{J} , \qquad U(F_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0{,}5357\ \text{J} , \qquad U(F_{\mathrm{x}}\ \text{and}\ F_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0{,}9099\ \text{J} .\]

The sum of the first two is only \(0{,}6378\) J, \(0{,}2721\) J less than the energy with both forces. The reason is the square in the formula for the energy (figure 4.417).

With both forces the force in a bar is the sum \(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} + N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\) of the forces caused by each force alone, and

\[\big(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} + N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\big)^2 = \big(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)}\big)^2 + 2\,N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)} + \big(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\big)^2 .\]

Let us draw this for the bar \(AC\). The side of the square is the force in the bar under both forces, \(1\) kN from \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\tfrac43\) kN from \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\). The area, multiplied by \(L_{\mathrm{AC}}/(2EA)\), is the energy of the bar. The small square is the energy \(0{,}1020\) J under the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) alone, the large square the energy \(0{,}1814\) J under the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) alone. These are the first and last terms. But the square with the side \(1 + \tfrac43\) also has two rectangles, each with \(0{,}1361\) J, which neither force gives alone. This is the middle term, the mixed energy \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)} L_{\mathrm{i}}/(EA)\). The bar \(BC\) carries no force under \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), so its square has no rectangles, and all of its \(0{,}3543\) J belong to the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\): \(U(F_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0{,}1814\ \text{J} + 0{,}3543\ \text{J} = 0{,}5357\) J. The mixed energy of the bracket is \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot \tfrac43\ \text{kN} \cdot 4\ \text{m}/(EA) + 0 \cdot \big({-\tfrac53}\ \text{kN}\big) \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 0{,}2721\) J. EP and CM say this explicitly: energy does not add up, because it is a quadratic function of the displacements or forces (EP, p. 220, CM §7.4.1, PDF p. 314). The mixed energy is exactly \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\ \text{µm} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 0{,}2721\) J. The next subsection shows that this is no coincidence.

4.8.3 The order of loading

Let us load the bracket slowly with the forces \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) kN to the right and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN upwards, first with the first and then with the second, and count the work the two forces do (figure 4.418, top). We need the work of a force that grows in proportion to the displacement of its point of application. The computation is the same as for the bar in theorem 4.3, only with a scalar product: if the force grows in proportion to the distance \(s\) from zero to \(\vek F\) on a displacement \(\Delta\vek u = \ell\,\vek d\) (\(\ell\) the length of the segment, \(\vek d\) the unit vector of its direction), the work is \(\int_0^\ell (s/\ell)\,\vek F\cdot\vek d\ \mathrm{d}s = \tfrac12\,\vek F\cdot\Delta\vek u\) (item 2 of definition 4.1 and the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55), half the work of the constant force \(\vek F\) on the same displacement. Now let us count.

  1. The force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) grows slowly from zero to 1 kN, the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) is not there yet. By (4.88) the joint moves along a straight segment, in proportion to the force, and at the end \(u = D_{\mathrm{xx}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 204{,}1\) µm and \(v = D_{\mathrm{yx}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\) µm. The force \((F_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\) counts only the horizontal part of the displacement, since its scalar product with the displacement is \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\,u\). By the computation above it does the work \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0{,}1020\) J, the area of the grey triangle at the top left of the figure.
  2. The force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) grows slowly from zero to 1 kN, while the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) stays 1 kN. The joint moves further by \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\) µm to the right and by \(D_{\mathrm{yy}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 1071{,}4\) µm up. The force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) does \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 1071{,}4\ \text{µm} = 0{,}5357\) J, the grey triangle at the top right. The force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the same throughout this stage and its point of application moves by 272,1 µm in its direction, so it does the work of a constant force, \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot 272{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0{,}2721\) J, the blue rectangle at the top left. There is no half here, because the force does not grow from zero, it is already fully present.
  3. The total work is \(0{,}1020\) + \(0{,}5357\) + \(0{,}2721\) J. With one more decimal this is \(0{,}10204 + 0{,}53571 + 0{,}27211 = 0{,}90986\) J, rounded \(0{,}9099\) J (the sum of the rounded numbers gives \(0{,}9098\) J). This is exactly the strain energy of the bracket with both forces, which we computed in subsection 4.8.2, as it must be for slow loading (section 4.1).

Now we apply the two forces in the opposite order (figure 4.418, bottom). First \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) grows and does \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 1071{,}4\ \text{µm} = 0{,}5357\) J, and the joint also moves by 272,1 µm to the right. Then \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) grows and does \(\tfrac12 \cdot 1\ \text{kN} \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0{,}1020\) J, while the joint moves further by \(D_{\mathrm{yx}} \cdot 1\ \text{kN} = 272{,}1\) µm up, and on this displacement the constant force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) does \(0{,}2721\) J. Together again \(0{,}9099\) J. We have now recognized the mixed energy of subsection 4.8.2. It is the work done by a force that is already fully present when the other force moves its point of application.

Let us write the same with letters, for forces \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) of any magnitude. With the order first \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), then \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), the work is

\[W_{\mathrm{I}} = \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + F_{\mathrm{x}}\,D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} ,\]

and with the opposite order

\[W_{\mathrm{II}} = \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + F_{\mathrm{y}}\,D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

The Roman numerals in the index give the order, they are not forces or directions. In both cases the final state is the same: by adding loads, the final forces in the bars and the final displacement of the joint with both forces are the same, regardless of which force came first. For the bracket we computed that the work in both cases equals the strain energy of the final state. In general we expect this because the work the material receives depends only on the final strain, not on the path (definition 3.58, item 2), and in slow loading the work of the forces is stored entirely in the material (section 4.1). If this is so, \(W_{\mathrm{I}} = W_{\mathrm{II}}\). The first two terms are the same in both expressions, so the last ones must be equal too, \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\,D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} = F_{\mathrm{y}}\,D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\), and for forces that are not zero \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

What would it mean if \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} \ne D_{\mathrm{yx}}\)? We would load the bracket in the first order and unload it in the reverse of the second order, first reducing \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and then \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\). When unloading along the same path backwards, the forces act in every state as in loading, but the displacements have the opposite sign, so the bracket gives back the work \(W_{\mathrm{II}}\). After such a cycle the bracket would be in the same state as at the start, but the forces would have done on it the work \(W_{\mathrm{I}} - W_{\mathrm{II}} = F_{\mathrm{x}} F_{\mathrm{y}}\,(D_{\mathrm{xy}} - D_{\mathrm{yx}})\), which is not zero. The cycle in the opposite direction would give the work \(W_{\mathrm{II}} - W_{\mathrm{I}}\). One of the two numbers would be negative, and in that cycle the bracket would give out work from nothing. This is forbidden by the same argument that we used for a small piece of material in section 3.6.4. The equality \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\) is therefore a consequence of the fact that an elastic body returns the work it receives.

This explanation is the explanation of EP and CM (EP §4.6.4, (4.6.22)-(4.6.24), pp. 226-227, CM §7.4.2, (7.4.11)-(7.4.13), PDF pp. 317-318). The two sources justify the equality of the works by the fact that at the end the body is loaded by the same pair of forces (EP, p. 227, CM, PDF p. 318). It uses, however, a conclusion that we have not yet proved for a body: that the work of the external forces in slow loading depends only on the final state, also when the ratio between the loads changes during loading, as in our two orders. For a bar we proved it in theorem 4.3, and for a body only for loads that all grow in proportion at the same time (corollary 4.87 on the work of the loads and the strain energy). Let us now prove it for a body.

First let us say what a path is. For the bracket the loads are the forces \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), which change during loading each in its own way. For a body, take \(m\) chosen loads \((\vek b^{(k)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(k)})\), \(k = 1, \dots, m\), with solutions \(\vek u^{(k)}\), and multiply them during loading by numbers \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\) that change. We describe the state by a parameter \(\lambda\), as in corollary 4.87, except that the factors are no longer all equal to \(\lambda\). For the bracket the chosen loads are the force of 1 kN in the direction \(x\) and the force of 1 kN in the direction \(y\), and the factors are the magnitudes of the forces in kilonewtons. The order first \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), then \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) is a path of two stages, the opposite order, first \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\), then \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), is another path. Both end at the point \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = F_{\mathrm{y}} = 1\) kN. On the first, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\lambda\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) for \(\lambda\) from \(0\) to \(\tfrac12\), on the second \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 2\lambda - 1\) for \(\lambda\) from \(\tfrac12\) to \(1\). But the two forces can also grow at the same time and at different rates, for example \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = \lambda\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = \lambda^2\) (figure 4.419, left). For every path, by the principle of superposition (lemma 4.135), the field \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek u^{(k)}\) is a solution for the load \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\,(\vek b^{(k)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(k)})\), and if the supports prevent every small rigid displacement, it is the only one by lemma 4.134 on the uniqueness of the solution. This is the state the body takes in slow loading, as in corollary 4.87.

What work do the loads do? The points no longer move along straight segments. On the path with \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = \lambda\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = \lambda^2\) the joint \(C\) moves along a curve (figure 4.419, right). On path I the displacement of the joint is a broken line, on path II another broken line, and all three paths end at the same point. Definition 4.1 counted the work only along a straight segment. We proceed as with every integral. On a short step of the parameter from \(\lambda\) to \(\lambda + \Delta\lambda\) the point \(P\) moves approximately by \(\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}(P, \lambda)\,\Delta\lambda\), where \(\partial\vek u/\partial\lambda\) is the derivative of the displacement of the point with respect to the parameter. A small piece of volume \(\Delta V\) at \(P\) carries the force of approximately \(\vek b(P, \lambda)\,\Delta V\), which hardly changes over the short step, so by item 1 of definition 4.1 it does the work of approximately \(\vek b\cdot\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}\,\Delta V\,\Delta\lambda\). The same holds for a patch of the surface. If for the work of a piece we assume the same as in step 3 of the proof of corollary 4.87 (between the least and the greatest value over the points of the piece), the work of the body on every step is an integral, and the sum over the steps turns into an integral over the parameter. This suggests the definition that follows. Books call such a sum along a curve a line integral, and KREYSZIG says that it is exactly the work of a force along a path (KREYSZIG §10.1, (3), PDF pp. 440-441). In section 4.1.1 we put it off, because proportional loads move the points along straight segments.

The figure shows the body at two neighbouring values of the parameter. The body is fixed at the support and carries a load, whose chosen parts we multiply by the factors \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\). The dashed shape is the body displaced at \(\lambda\), the full shape is the body at \(\lambda + \Delta\lambda\). The point \(P\) moves between them by \(\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}\,\Delta\lambda\), and we shall use this derivative of the displacement with respect to the parameter as the virtual displacement.

Definition 4.136 Loading path and the work along it (pot obremenjevanja in delo na njej)

Let the body be as in definition 4.133, let \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}), \dots, (\vek b^{(m)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(m)})\) be loads of the body with solutions \(\vek u^{(1)}, \dots, \vek u^{(m)}\), and let \(\kappa_1, \dots, \kappa_{\mathrm{m}}\) be functions that are differentiable on an open interval \(J\) containing the closed interval \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\) and have derivatives continuous on \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\).

  1. A loading path (pot obremenjevanja) is the family of loads and displacement fields
    \[\vek b(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\vek b^{(k)} , \qquad \bar{\vek t}(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\bar{\vek t}^{(k)} , \qquad \vek u(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^m \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\vek u^{(k)}\]
    for \(\lambda \in [\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\).
  2. The work of the loads (delo obremenitev) along this path is the number
    \[W_{\mathrm{zun}} = \int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda_1} \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b(\lambda)\cdot\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}(\lambda)\cdot\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}A \bigg)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda , \tag{4.89}\]
    where \(\partial\vek u/\partial\lambda = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}'(\lambda)\,\vek u^{(k)}\) is the derivative of the displacement of every point with respect to the parameter \(\lambda\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.1, (3) (PDF pp. 440-441), where the work of a force along a path is a line integral, EP (3.1.2) (p. 97). The path as a sum of chosen loads with variable factors is not from the sources.

The integral in (4.89) exists. By the linearity of the integral over the body and over the surface (section 4.2), the expression in brackets equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}'(\lambda)\,W_{\mathrm{kl}}\), where

\[W_{\mathrm{kl}} = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(k)}\cdot\vek u^{(l)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(k)}\cdot\vek u^{(l)}\,\mathrm{d}A \tag{4.90}\]

is the work that the load \(k\) would do on the displacements of the solution \(l\) if it stayed the same all the time. The letter \(W\) with two indices is a work, not the weight of the hanging bar. The expression in brackets is therefore a sum of products of continuous functions of the parameter with constant numbers, a continuous function on \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\) (corollary 1.65), and by theorem 3.53 it has an integral. The definition agrees with corollary 4.87. For a single load with \(\kappa_1(\lambda) = \lambda\) on \([0, 1]\) the expression in brackets is \(\lambda\,W_{11}\), and the work is \(\int_0^1 \lambda\,W_{11}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda = \tfrac12\,W_{11}\), as in the corollary. Now we can state the theorem.

The figure shows how the energy changes with the parameter. On the axes of the left graph are \(w\) and \(\lambda\), on the axes of the middle graph \(U\) and \(\lambda\), on the axes of the right graph \(U'\) and \(\lambda\), each with the limits \(\lambda_0\) and \(\lambda_1\). On the left is the energy density \(w(\lambda)\) at the point \(P\), its derivative at a chosen \(\lambda\) is the slope of the tangent. In the middle is the energy of the body \(U(\lambda)\), which starts at \(\lambda_0\), its derivative is the slope of the tangent, and the difference \(U(\lambda_1) - U(\lambda_0)\) is the height between start and end. On the right is the derivative \(U'(\lambda)\), and its area is the same difference. The theorem that follows states exactly this.

Theorem 4.137 Work along any loading path (delo pri poljubni poti obremenjevanja)

Let the loading path be as in definition 4.136, the material ideal elastic and linear elastic, and let the strains of the field \(\vek u(\lambda)\) be small at every point of the body for every \(\lambda \in [\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\). Let \(U(\lambda)\) be the strain energy of the body (definition 4.85) at the displacement field \(\vek u(\lambda)\). Then the work of the loads along the path equals the difference of the strain energies in the final and in the initial state,

\[W_{\mathrm{zun}} = U(\lambda_1) - U(\lambda_0) . \tag{4.91}\]

If all factors are zero at the start, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda_0) = 0\) for all \(k\), then \(W_{\mathrm{zun}} = U(\lambda_1)\), the strain energy of the final state.

Proof

We have to show that the expression in brackets in (4.89) is the derivative of the function \(U\), and then use the fundamental theorem of calculus. We get the derivative from the principle of virtual displacements with the virtual displacement \(\partial\vek u/\partial\lambda\).

  1. The state at every \(\lambda\). By the principle of superposition (lemma 4.135), applied to every term of the sum, \(\vek u(\lambda)\) is a solution for the load \((\vek b(\lambda), \bar{\vek t}(\lambda))\), with the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\varepsilon^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\sigma^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(\varepsilon^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(\sigma^{(k)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the strains and stresses of the solution \(\vek u^{(k)}\).
  2. The virtual displacement. Choose \(\lambda \in [\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\) and take \(\delta\vek u = \partial\vek u/\partial\lambda = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \kappa_{\mathrm{l}}'(\lambda)\,\vek u^{(l)}\). As in step 1 of the proof of lemma 4.135 on the principle of superposition, this field is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the body with its surface, and it is \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.79). By step 2 of the same proof its virtual strain is \(\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \kappa_{\mathrm{l}}'(\lambda)\,\varepsilon^{(l)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  3. The principle of virtual displacements. The stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\lambda)\) are the stresses of a solution, so they are continuously differentiable, satisfy the equilibrium equations with the body force \(\vek b(\lambda)\) and on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the Cauchy formula with \(\bar{\vek t}(\lambda)\). They are symmetric, because \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}}\) (lemma 3.26, item 2). By theorem 4.82 on the principle of virtual displacements, therefore,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\lambda)\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b(\lambda)\cdot\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}(\lambda)\cdot\frac{\partial\vek u}{\partial\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
    The right side is the expression in brackets in (4.89).
  4. The energy density at a point. At a point \(P\) of the body the strain at \(\lambda\) is small by assumption, so by theorem 3.62 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, item 2, \(w(\lambda) = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}(\lambda)\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}(\lambda)\), where \(\{\varepsilon\}(\lambda)\) is the Voigt column of the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(\lambda)\) (definition 3.27). By step 1, \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\{\varepsilon^{(k)}\}_{\mathrm{p}}\). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82), therefore, \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) is differentiable on \(J\) with the derivative \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}'(\lambda)\,\{\varepsilon^{(k)}\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), which by step 2 is the component \(\{\delta\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) of the Voigt column of the virtual strain.
  5. Let now \(\lambda\) be an interior point of the interval, \(\lambda_0 < \lambda < \lambda_1\). On the interval \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\) the formula of step 4 holds, while outside it the strains may be large and the formula is not guaranteed. The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient \((w(\lambda + h) - w(\lambda))/h\), the slope of a secant, as \(h\) goes to zero. For every \(h\) that is in absolute value smaller than the distance to the nearer end point, \(\lambda + h\) lies in the band, so the limit uses only values given by the formula. From the end point \(\lambda_1\), however, a secant to the right would leave the band, so we compute the derivatives of steps 5, 7 and 8 only on the open interval \((\lambda_0, \lambda_1)\), and this is enough for the fundamental theorem of calculus in step 9. By the product rule the derivative of the density with respect to \(\lambda\) is
    \[\frac{\mathrm{d}w}{\mathrm{d}\lambda} = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\delta\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} + \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\delta\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}} .\]
    By theorem 3.62, item 1, \(C_{\mathrm{pq}} = C_{\mathrm{qp}}\), so the second sum, after swapping the indices \(p\) and \(q\), equals the first. Hence \(\mathrm{d}w/\mathrm{d}\lambda = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \big(\sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{q}}\big)\,\{\delta\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}} = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \{\sigma\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\delta\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}\), which by (3.67), applied to products, is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\lambda)\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the integrand on the left in step 3.
  6. The energy as a function of the parameter. We insert \(\{\varepsilon\}_{\mathrm{p}}(\lambda) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\{\varepsilon^{(k)}\}_{\mathrm{p}}\) into the density of step 4:
    \[w(\lambda) = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}(\lambda)\,B_{\mathrm{kl}} , \qquad B_{\mathrm{kl}} = \sum_{\mathrm{p}} \sum_{\mathrm{q}} C_{\mathrm{pq}}\,\{\varepsilon^{(k)}\}_{\mathrm{p}}\,\{\varepsilon^{(l)}\}_{\mathrm{q}} .\]
    The functions \(B_{\mathrm{kl}}\) depend only on the point and are continuous on the body, because the strains of the solutions are continuous (corollary 1.70, item 1). By the linearity of the integral over the body (section 4.2), \(U(\lambda) = \tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}(\lambda)\,U_{\mathrm{kl}}\), where \(U_{\mathrm{kl}} = \int_{\mathrm{V}} B_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\mathrm{d}V\) are constant numbers.
  7. The derivative of the energy. The formula for \(U\) of step 6 holds on \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\), so by the rules of differentiation \(U\) is differentiable at every point of the open interval \((\lambda_0, \lambda_1)\), for the same reason as \(w\) in step 5, and
    \[U'(\lambda) = \frac12 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \big(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}'(\lambda)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}(\lambda) + \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda)\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}'(\lambda)\big)\,U_{\mathrm{kl}} .\]
    By the same rules the derivative of the density of step 6 is \(\tfrac12 \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} (\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}'\kappa_{\mathrm{l}} + \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}')\,B_{\mathrm{kl}}\) at every point, and by the linearity of the integral over the body the integral of this derivative over the body is \(U'(\lambda)\).
  8. Steps 5 and 7 computed the derivative of the same function \(\lambda \mapsto w(\lambda)\) at the same point in two ways. The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient, and a limit is unique (lemma 1.7), so the two expressions are equal. The integral of the left side of step 3 is therefore \(U'(\lambda)\), and by step 3 the expression in brackets in (4.89) equals \(U'(\lambda)\) for every \(\lambda \in (\lambda_0, \lambda_1)\).
  9. We denote the expression in brackets in (4.89) by \(f(\lambda)\). Right after definition 4.136 we showed that \(f\) is continuous on \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\), and by step 8, \(f(\lambda) = U'(\lambda)\) for every \(\lambda \in (\lambda_0, \lambda_1)\). By step 6, on \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\) the function \(U\) is a sum of products of the functions \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}\) with constant numbers. The functions \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuous because they are differentiable (lemma 1.80), so \(U\) is continuous on \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\) (corollary 1.65). These are the hypotheses of the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 1, with \(G = U\), which needs the derivative only at interior points, and the area under \(f\) is
    \[W_{\mathrm{zun}} = \int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda_1} f(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda = U(\lambda_1) - U(\lambda_0) .\]
  10. If all \(\kappa_{\mathrm{k}}(\lambda_0) = 0\), then by step 6 \(U(\lambda_0) = 0\), and \(W_{\mathrm{zun}} = U(\lambda_1)\).

Source: EP §4.6.4 (pp. 226-227) and CM §7.4.2 (PDF pp. 317-318) state the equality of the works for two orders of loading, and SADD §6.1 (PDF p. 130) says that the work does not depend on the order of loading. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof showed where the independence of the path comes from. The principle of virtual displacements with the virtual displacement \(\partial\vek u/\partial\lambda\) says that the work of the loads on a short step of the path equals the work of the stresses on the change of the strains. Step 5 says that this work of the stresses is exactly the change of the energy density, \(\mathrm{d}w/\mathrm{d}\lambda = \sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\). This is the relation between the stresses and the derivatives of the energy density of lemma 3.61, written along the path. In step 5 we used the symmetry \(C_{\mathrm{pq}} = C_{\mathrm{qp}}\). Without it the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) would not be the derivative of any function of the state, and the work would depend on the path, as for the imagined material with \(C_{16} \ne C_{61}\) of section 3.6.4. The assumption of small strains enters in step 4. Only for them is the energy density half the sum of the products (theorem 3.62, item 2), and only for them does the principle of virtual displacements hold in the form of step 3 (section 4.5). For the steel of our examples the strain up to the yield stress 220 MPa is at most \(0{,}0011\) (section 4.6.2), so the assumption excludes rubber and similar materials, not steel in its elastic range. We require it only on the interval \([\lambda_0, \lambda_1]\), and that is why in step 5 we differentiated only at interior points. We proved the theorem for a linear elastic material and for loads that are sums of chosen loads with variable factors. This is a simplification. For a nonlinear ideal elastic material the principle of superposition does not hold, so we would not get the states by adding as in step 1. We would have to assume that the body takes an equilibrium state at every \(\lambda\) and that its displacements change continuously differentiably with \(\lambda\), and step 5 would need the chain rule for a function of six variables (LEBL2 theorem 8.3.7, PDF p. 38). For a load that changes its shape during loading, for example a truck driving across a bridge, step 6 does not hold, and the derivative of the energy would need differentiation under the integral over the body. Lemma 4.19 gives it only for an integral over an interval, and LEBL2 also only for such an integral (theorem 9.1.1, PDF pp. 65-66). For a body one would prove it with uniform continuity in the point and the parameter at the same time, which we do not develop in the book.

A path of several stages, like our two orders, is not a path in the sense of definition 4.136. Figure 4.423, left, shows the factors of the order first \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\), then \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) against \(\lambda\). At \(\lambda = \tfrac12\) their derivatives jump: the slope of the factor \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}}\) drops from 2 to 0, the slope of the factor \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}}\) rises from 0 to 2. The theorem holds, however, on each stage separately. On the right is the energy of the bracket along this path. On the first stage the factors \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = 2\lambda\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\) are polynomials, differentiable at all numbers, and the theorem on the interval \([0, \tfrac12]\) gives the work \(U(\tfrac12) - U(0)\), for the bracket \(0{,}10204\) J, the work of the force \(F_{\mathrm{x}}\) of step 1 at the start of the section. On the second stage \(\kappa_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{y}} = 2\lambda - 1\) are polynomials too, and the theorem on \([\tfrac12, 1]\) gives \(U(1) - U(\tfrac12)\), for the bracket \(0{,}53571 + 0{,}27211 = 0{,}80782\) J of step 2. The sum is \(U(1) - U(0) = U(1)\), for the bracket \(0{,}90986\) J. The intermediate state \(U(\tfrac12)\) is the end of the first stage and the start of the second, so it cancels. The same holds for the opposite order, with another intermediate state and the same end, and for every path of finitely many stages. Therefore \(W_{\mathrm{I}} = W_{\mathrm{II}}\) for every body of a linear and ideal elastic material, and the explanation by the order of loading has become a proof. The expression in brackets in (4.89) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}}\sum_{\mathrm{l}} \kappa_{\mathrm{k}}\,\kappa_{\mathrm{l}}'\,W_{\mathrm{kl}}\), so for two loads of a body, on the stages of the order first \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\), then \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\), we get \(W_{\mathrm{I}} = \tfrac12\,W_{11} + \tfrac12\,W_{22} + W_{12}\), and for the opposite order \(W_{\mathrm{II}} = \tfrac12\,W_{22} + \tfrac12\,W_{11} + W_{21}\). From \(W_{\mathrm{I}} = W_{\mathrm{II}}\) it follows that \(W_{12} = W_{21}\): the work of the first load on the displacements of the second equals the work of the second on the displacements of the first.

The bracket is not a body, but the computation is the same. On the path \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = \lambda\) kN and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = \lambda^2\) kN the displacement of the joint is, by (4.88), \(u = 204{,}1\,\lambda + 272{,}1\,\lambda^2\) and \(v = 272{,}1\,\lambda + 1071{,}4\,\lambda^2\) in micrometres (figure 4.419, right). The work of the forces is the sum of the works of the two forces along the path of the joint, \(\int_0^1 (F_{\mathrm{x}}\,u' + F_{\mathrm{y}}\,v')\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\), where the prime means the derivative with respect to \(\lambda\). With SymPy we get \(0{,}9099\) J, exactly as for both orders. Why? By (4.88) the integrand is
