\[F_{\mathrm{x}}\,u' + F_{\mathrm{y}}\,v' = D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}' + D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}' + D_{\mathrm{yx}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}' + D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}' .\]

The first and the last term are the derivatives of the functions \(\tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) and \(\tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}^2\). The two middle terms together, however, are the derivative of the function \(D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}\), whose derivative is \(D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,(F_{\mathrm{x}}'\,F_{\mathrm{y}} + F_{\mathrm{x}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}')\), only when \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\). For the bracket this is so, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus the work along every path equals \(\tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{xx}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + D_{\mathrm{xy}}\,F_{\mathrm{x}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}} + \tfrac12\,D_{\mathrm{yy}}\,F_{\mathrm{y}}^2\) at the final forces, \(\tfrac12 \cdot 204{,}1 + 272{,}1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 1071{,}4 = 909{,}9\) µm kN \(= 0{,}9099\) J. For the bracket the role of the symmetry \(C_{\mathrm{pq}} = C_{\mathrm{qp}}\) of step 5 is played by the equality \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

The next subsection proves the relation \(W_{12} = W_{21}\) also directly, without a loading path, from the principle of virtual displacements and the symmetry of the elastic constants.

4.8.4 Betti's theorem

Take a body with supports on a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) of its surface, let the rest of the surface be \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), and two loads (figure 4.424). The first, \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\), causes the displacement field \(\vek u^{(1)}\), the second, \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\), the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\). The work that the forces of the first load would do if they stayed the same while their points of application move by \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is, by definition 4.1 for one point and the same assumption for the pieces of the body and of the surface as in step 3 of the proof of corollary 4.87 (see also the potential energy of the loads in section 4.6.3), equal to

\[W_{12} = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]

The first index says which load works, the second on whose displacements. The letter \(W\) with two indices is a work, not the weight of the hanging bar. For the bracket this work was the blue rectangle in figure 4.418, the work of the first force on the displacement caused by the second. In figure 4.424 this is the displacement \(\vek u^{(2)}\) of the point where the first load acts, and conversely the displacement \(\vek u^{(1)}\) of the point where the second acts.

Before we state the theorem, let us look inside the body, where the proof is decided (figure 4.425). The principle of virtual displacements will turn the external works \(W_{12}\) and \(W_{21}\) into the work of the stresses of one load on the strains of the other, piece by piece. So take from the body a small cube with an edge of length 1 and deform it in two ways. We look at it along the axis \(z\), so that the axis \(x\) points to the right and the axis \(y\) up. First we stretch it only in the direction \(x\), so that the edge gets longer by \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\), while the height stays the same. The material would like to get narrower as this happens, so the height is kept by the stress \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yy}} = C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\) on the top and bottom faces, as the generalized Hooke's law says (definition 3.25), in which a single term of the sum remains. Second we stretch the cube only in the direction \(y\), by \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and the width is kept by the stress \(\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\) on the left and right faces.

Now we multiply crosswise. The stress of the first deformation acts on the top and bottom faces, and exactly these two faces move apart by \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\) in the second deformation. A face has the area \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\), so the force on it is numerically equal to the stress, and on this displacement it would do the work

\[\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}} = C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\]

on a cube of unit volume. Conversely, the stress of the second deformation on the displacement of the first would do the work

\[\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} = C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} .\]

The two products differ only in the constant, \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\) or \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\). When the constants are equal, the works are equal. This is the whole of Betti's theorem in the small: the proof adds such crosswise products over all components and over the whole body.

Why does only the stress \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\) work in the second deformation? The first deformation has other stresses too (figure 4.426), the stress \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\) on the left and right faces, the stress \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{zz}}\) on the front face, which we are looking at, and on the back face, and for an anisotropic material also shear stresses, for example \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xy}} = C_{\mathrm{xyxx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The figure shows them on the cube during the second deformation, when every point moves only up, at height \(y\) by \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,y\). A force in the direction \(x\) or \(z\) therefore does no work, because no point moves in that direction. Such are the stress \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the shear stress on the top and bottom faces and the stress \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The shear stress on the left and right faces points in the direction \(y\), but the points of the two faces at the same height move equally, and the two forces point in opposite directions. The points of each of these faces move from 0 at the bottom to \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\) at the top, on average by half of it, so the shear stress on the right face does the work \(+\tfrac12\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and on the left face \(-\tfrac12\,\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and the two works cancel. The same holds for the shear stress in the direction \(y\) on the front and back faces. Together these stresses do no work, so figure 4.425 does not show them.

Theorem 4.138 Betti's reciprocal theorem (Bettijev izrek)

Let the body be as in definition 4.133, of an ideal elastic material. Let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(1)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(1)})\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) a solution for the load \((\vek b^{(2)}, \bar{\vek t}^{(2)})\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} &\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ &\qquad = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}A . \end{aligned} \tag{4.92}\]
Proof

We must show that both sides equal the same integral of stresses and strains. We get each side from the principle of virtual displacements, taking as the virtual displacement the solution for the other load, and the equality of the two integrals from the symmetry of the elastic constants, which on the cube means the equality of \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\).

  1. By requirement 1 of definition 4.133 the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the body with its surface, and equal to \(\vek 0\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), since at the wall the orange shape coincides with the blackwhite one, so it is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.79). The definition does not require the virtual displacement to be small. The components of the small strain tensor of the field \(\delta\vek u = \vek u^{(2)}\) are the strains \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) of the solution, because they are computed from the same partial derivatives.
  2. By requirements 2 and 3 the stresses \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuously differentiable, satisfy the equilibrium equations with the body force \(\vek b^{(1)}\) and, on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), Cauchy's formula with the traction vector \(\bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\). They are symmetric, because \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{jikl}}\) (lemma 3.26, item 2). These are the assumptions of the principle of virtual displacements (theorem 4.82), which with the virtual displacement \(\vek u^{(2)}\) gives
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(1)}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
    The right side is the left side of equation (4.92), the forces of the first load on the displacements of the second.
  3. In the same way, with the roles of the two loads exchanged, the principle for the second load with the virtual displacement \(\vek u^{(1)}\) gives
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}^{(2)}\cdot\vek u^{(1)}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    and the right side is the right side of equation (4.92). It remains to show that the left sides of steps 2 and 3 are equal.
  4. At every point of the body \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\) by definition 3.25, so
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]
    One of the 81 terms of this sum is the product of figure 4.425, the stress of the first times the strain of the second, the term with \(i = j = y\) and \(k = l = x\).
  5. The material is ideal elastic and linear elastic, so by theorem 3.62 on the symmetry of the elastic constants, item 1, \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) for all indices. We insert this:
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \Big( \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{klij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} \Big)\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}} ,\]
    where we exchanged the order of the finite sums and took \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\) out of the sum over \(i\) and \(j\). For the term of figure 4.425 this is the exchange of \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\) for \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\).
  6. By definition 3.25, written for the pair of indices \(kl\) instead of \(ij\), the expression in the bracket is the stress \(\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\) of the second solution, in figure 4.425 the stress \(\sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which now multiplies the strain of the first. The right side of step 5 is therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \sum_{\mathrm{l}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{kl}}\). When we rename the indices, \(k\) to \(i\) and \(l\) to \(j\), this is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  7. The integrands on the left sides of steps 2 and 3 are therefore equal at every point, on the cube stress of the first times strain of the second and stress of the second times strain of the first, so the integrals are equal too. The right sides of steps 2 and 3 are therefore equal, which is (4.92).

Source: EP theorem 4.6.2, (4.6.25)-(4.6.27) (pp. 227-228), SADD §6.4.2, (6.4.2), (6.4.3) (PDF pp. 135-136), CM §7.4.2, (7.4.14)-(7.4.18) (PDF pp. 318-319), BOWER §5.8.1 (PDF pp. 379-380). In steps 2 and 3 the sources use the divergence theorem directly, which in our case the principle of virtual displacements has already used.

This is Betti's reciprocal theorem. The work \(W_{12}\) of the first load on the displacements of the second equals the work \(W_{21}\) of the second load on the displacements of the first. The proof showed which properties of the body are needed for this. The principle of virtual displacements knows nothing about the material and holds for every body in equilibrium. The material enters in step 2 through the symmetry of the stresses, and in steps 4 to 6 through the linear Hooke's law and the symmetry \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\), which we derived in section 3.6 from the requirement that the material returns the work it receives. In figure 4.425 this is the equality of the constants in the one and the other stress. This is the precise form of the explanation with the order of loading.

For an isotropic material the symmetry is directly visible. By Hooke's law (3.28), \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \lambda\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when \(i = j\), and \(\sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\) when \(i \ne j\), where \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}} = \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants (definition 3.18). The sum in step 2 is therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} &= \lambda\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}}\,\big(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{zz}}\big) + 2\mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} \\ &= \lambda\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{v}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{v}} + 2\mu \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{ij}} , \end{aligned}\]

an expression that does not change if we exchange the labels (1) and (2). For the cube of figure 4.425 both constants equal \(\lambda\), \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}} = \lambda\) and \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}} = \lambda\).

And what if, for example, \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}} \ne C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\)? Take a first strain whose only nonzero component is \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and a second whose only nonzero component is \(\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\), as in figure 4.425. In the sum of step 4 only the term with \(i = j = y\) and \(k = l = x\) remains, that is \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and with the roles exchanged only \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The two sums would differ, and the theorem would not hold. With numbers: imagine a material with \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}} = 110\) GPa and \(C_{\mathrm{xxyy}} = 100\) GPa and take \(\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0{,}001\). Then

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma^{(1)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}} &= 110\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}001 \cdot 0{,}001 = 110\ \text{kJ/m}^3 , \\ \sigma^{(2)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 100\ \text{GPa} \cdot 0{,}001 \cdot 0{,}001 = 100\ \text{kJ/m}^3 . \end{aligned}\]

The difference, 10 kJ per cubic metre, is exactly the work of the cycle in figure 4.427, left, in the plane of the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) of the cube. We stretch the cube in the direction \(x\) by 0,001, then also in the direction \(y\) by 0,001, and take both stretches away again in the same order, until the cube is as it was at the start. The work of the stresses on the cube on each of the four legs is drawn on the right as a step that adds or subtracts its part. On the second leg the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) due to the first stretch does the work \(C_{\mathrm{yyxx}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}} = 110\) kJ/m³, and on the third the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) due to the second stretch the work \(-C_{\mathrm{xxyy}}\,\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\varepsilon^{(1)}_{\mathrm{xx}} = -100\) kJ/m³. All other contributions cancel between loading and unloading. The part of the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) caused by the stretch in the direction \(x\) has on the third leg, at every value of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the same value as on the first, while the stretch now decreases. So its work on the third leg, \(-\tfrac12 C_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), is the opposite of the work \(+\tfrac12 C_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) on the first. The same holds for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) on the second and fourth legs. What remains is \(110 - 100 = 10\) kJ/m³. In this cycle such a material would receive 10 kJ/m³ of work and not return it, and in the reversed cycle it would give out as much work from nothing, like the imagined material with \(C_{16} \ne C_{61}\) in section 3.6.4. SADD mentions that Truesdell proved the theorem to be even a necessary and sufficient condition for an elastic material to have a strain energy density (SADD, PDF p. 136).

When does the theorem fail (figure 4.428)? First, when the supports prescribe displacements that are not zero, for example when the wall settles under the second load. Then the support forces on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) do work, and in the proof the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is not a kinematically admissible virtual displacement. SADD therefore integrates the traction vector over the whole surface \(S\) in the theorem, where on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) it is the force of the support (SADD (6.4.2), PDF p. 135). For fixed supports these terms are zero, because the displacement there is zero, and we get (4.92). Second, for a material without symmetric elastic constants, as we have just seen. Third, when adding loads fails: for large displacements, for a nonlinear material, whose stress for the sum of two strains is not the sum of the two stresses, and for loads that change with the deformation, since there the principle of virtual displacements or Hooke's law in the form we used does not hold. How small are the displacements of the bracket that follows? Under the load the joint \(C\) goes down by 10,714 mm at the end of the bar \(AC\), 4 m long, so the direction of the bar turns by about \(10{,}714/4000 = 0{,}0027\) radians. The axial force \(N\) in the bar is therefore no longer horizontal, its vertical component is about \(0{,}0027\,N\). Equilibrium written on the shape before loading leaves this component out and is therefore off by a few thousandths of the forces. By this much the model of small displacements, in which the theorem holds exactly, differs from the real bracket.

Let us test the theorem on the bracket of section 4.8.1 (figure 4.429). The bracket is not a body but a model of bars, and the same statement holds for it with the same proof.

In the figure the pins \(A\) and \(B\) on the wall and the bracket before loading are the same under both loads. Instead of the principle of virtual displacements for a body we use the principle for the truss (4.50), \(N_{\mathrm{AC}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{AC}} + N_{\mathrm{BC}}\,\delta e_{\mathrm{BC}} = \vek F\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\), where \(\delta e = \vek n\cdot\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) is the virtual elongation of a bar (equation (4.49)). For the first load, the force \(\vek F^{(1)}\) at the joint, we take as the virtual displacement of the joint its actual displacement under the second load, \(\delta\vek u_{\mathrm{C}} = \vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)}\). The virtual elongations are then the actual elongations \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{i}}^{(2)}\) of the bars under the second load (step 4 of section 4.8.1), and by step 3 of the same section the axial forces of the bars under the first load are \(N_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)} = EA\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{i}}^{(1)}/L_{\mathrm{i}}\). Therefore

\[\frac{EA}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(1)}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(2)} + \frac{EA}{L_{\mathrm{BC}}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}^{(1)}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}^{(2)} = \vek F^{(1)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)} .\]

The left side does not change if we exchange the labels (1) and (2), so \(\vek F^{(1)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)} = \vek F^{(2)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(1)}\). The role of the symmetric elastic constants is played here by the numbers \(EA/L_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(EA/L_{\mathrm{BC}}\), by which each force in a bar is connected only with the elongation of the same bar.

We can compute the left side too. By step 4 of section 4.8.1, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}} = u\) and \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}} = \tfrac45\,u - \tfrac35\,v\). The bar \(AC\) gets shorter under the load, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(1)} = -2721\) µm, and gets longer under the horizontal force, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(2)} = 204{,}1\) µm. The bar \(BC\) carries no force under the horizontal force and keeps its length, \(\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}^{(2)} = \tfrac45 \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} - \tfrac35 \cdot 272{,}1\ \text{µm} = 0\), so the second term drops out. With \(EA/L_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\ \text{N}/4\ \text{m} = 4{,}9 \cdot 10^6\) N/m there remains

\[\frac{EA}{L_{\mathrm{AC}}}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(1)}\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^{(2)} = 4{,}9 \cdot 10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} \cdot (-2721\ \text{µm}) \cdot 204{,}1\ \text{µm} = -2{,}721\ \text{J} .\]

Both external works must give this number.

Let us check them. The first load is the load from the beginning of the chapter, \(\vek F^{(1)} = (0, -10, 0)\) kN, the second a horizontal force \(\vek F^{(2)} = (1, 0, 0)\) kN. By (4.88) the displacement of the joint has under the first load the components \(u^{(1)} = -2721\) µm and \(v^{(1)} = -10\,714\) µm, and under the second \(u^{(2)} = 204{,}1\) µm and \(v^{(2)} = 272{,}1\) µm. The scalar product picks from a displacement only the part in the direction of the force, the blue part in the figure. The two works are

\[\begin{aligned} W_{12} &= \vek F^{(1)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(2)} = (-10\ \text{kN}) \cdot 272{,}1\ \text{µm} = -2{,}721\ \text{J} , \\ W_{21} &= \vek F^{(2)}\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}^{(1)} = 1\ \text{kN} \cdot (-2721\ \text{µm}) = -2{,}721\ \text{J} . \end{aligned}\]

Both works are negative. The horizontal force lifts the joint, against the load that pulls down. The load in turn pushes the joint towards the wall, against the horizontal force that pulls to the right. The works are equal, although they are products of very different numbers, a large force of 10 kN with a small rise of 272,1 µm and a small force of 1 kN with a large displacement of 2721 µm.

Let us also test it on loads that do not act at a point (figure 4.430). Let the steel bar of chapter 1, of length \(L = 10\) m, with the cross-sectional area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa, be held at its top cross section, and let the axis \(x\) point down from it. We describe it with the bar model of section 4.4, in which the whole cross section at \(x\) moves down by \(u(x)\), as in section 4.6.2. The first load is the weight of the bar, per unit length \(q = \rho g A\), with \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ and \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s². We know the displacement it causes from chapter 1, \(u^{(1)}(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = \rho g/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) (section 3.1.10). The second load is a force \(F\) at the lower end, without the weight. Then every cross section carries the force \(F\), the strain is \(F/(EA)\) everywhere, and the displacement is \(u^{(2)}(x) = F x/(EA)\).

The work of the weight on the displacements of the second load is the sum of the works of the weights of the small pieces, \(q\,\Delta x\), on the displacement \(u^{(2)}(x)\), in the limit an integral. The work of the force \(F\) on the displacements of the first load is \(F\) times the displacement of the lower end, \(u^{(1)}(L)\):

\[\begin{aligned} W_{12} &= \int_0^L \rho g A \cdot \frac{F x}{EA}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho g F}{E}\cdot\frac{L^2}{2} , \\ W_{21} &= F\,u^{(1)}(L) = F\,a\,(2L \cdot L - L^2) = F\,\frac{\rho g}{2E}\,L^2 . \end{aligned}\]

We computed the first integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus, since \(x^2/2\) has the derivative \(x\). Both works are \(\rho g F L^2/(2E)\), for \(F = 1\) kN this is \(0{,}01952\) J, the force of 1 kN times the displacement of the end, 19,52 µm. Here too the theorem holds with the same proof as for a body. In the principle of virtual displacements for a bar (theorem 4.76), \(\int_0^L N\,\delta u'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,\delta u\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,\delta u(L)\), we take \(\delta u = u^{(2)}\) for the first load and \(\delta u = u^{(1)}\) for the second. Both fields are polynomials, so they have a continuous derivative, as the theorem requires, and both are zero at \(x = 0\). The axial force of a linear elastic bar is \(N = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} A = E A\,u'\) (definition 3.1), so the left side for the first load is \(\int_0^L EA\,(u^{(1)})'\,(u^{(2)})'\,\mathrm{d}x\), and for the second \(\int_0^L EA\,(u^{(2)})'\,(u^{(1)})'\,\mathrm{d}x\), the same integral. The role of the elastic constants is played here by the single number \(EA\), and the product does not change if we exchange the labels (1) and (2).

What does the theorem give us here? Suppose we knew only the simple field \(u^{(2)}\) of the end force, but not the displacement due to the weight. The theorem would give us the displacement of the lower end due to the weight without solving the problem with the weight:

\[u^{(1)}(L) = \frac{W_{12}}{F} = \int_0^L \rho g A\,\frac{x}{EA}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho g L^2}{2E} = \frac{7800 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 10^2}{2 \cdot 196 \cdot 10^9}\ \text{m} = 19{,}52\ \text{µm} ,\]

which is \(a L^2\), as in chapter 1. In figure 4.430 we exchanged the blue area under the straight line, multiplied by the weight per unit length and divided by \(F\), for the blue point at the end of the parabola. This is how EP uses the theorem for the bending of bars, which we will meet in chapter 5: the displacement of the end due to a force at the end is known, and the displacement of the end due to a distributed load is sought (EP example 4.6.5, p. 229). EP and CM also check the theorem on the same pair of loads (EP example 4.6.4, pp. 228-229, CM example 7.4.4, PDF pp. 319-320).

4.8.5 Maxwell's theorem

Betti's theorem compares the works of whole loads. The simplest load is a single force, and for the bracket we got \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = D_{\mathrm{yx}}\) for two such loads. How do we state this for a body? A force at a single point of a body is an idealization that does not work well in a body. SADD writes the displacement of an unbounded isotropic body due to a force at one point, and at the distance \(r\) from the point it is proportional to \(1/r\) (SADD (6.4.5), PDF p. 136). As \(r\) approaches zero it grows beyond all bounds, and the displacement of the point itself is not a finite number. We therefore spread the force over a small patch of the surface, and as the displacement we take the average of the displacements of the patch in the direction of the force. For the bracket and for the bar, where the forces act at joints and on cross sections, this is not necessary, and there the displacement of the point of application is a finite number.

How do we spread the force? Look at the section through the patch along the axis \(x\) on the top face of the body. The simplest way would be evenly, with a traction vector equal to the force divided by the area of the patch on the patch and zero elsewhere. Such a load, however, jumps to zero at the edge of the patch, and a solution with continuously differentiable stresses as in definition 4.133 cannot carry it. The normal of a flat face is the same on both sides of the edge, so a continuous stress gives the same traction vector \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n\) on both sides, as we said at assumption 3 in section 4.5.1. We therefore spread the force with a weight, a function that is largest in the middle of the patch and falls continuously to zero towards the edge, like the bump of lemma 4.123 (figure 4.432). The traction vector is the force times the weight, divided by the integral of the weight over the surface. In this way the total force is exactly \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\). With the same weight we compute the average of the displacements of the patch. Why with the same one? Because then the work of the load on the displacements is exactly the force times this average, and this is just what we will need in the proof of the equality \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = D_{\mathrm{ji}}\).

Definition 4.139 Flexibility matrix (podajnostna matrika)

Let the body be as in lemma 4.134 on the uniqueness of the solution, with supports that prevent every small rigid displacement of it, and let patches \(\Delta S_1, \dots, \Delta S_{\mathrm{m}}\) of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), unit vectors \(\vek d_1, \dots, \vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\) and weights \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{\mathrm{m}}\) be chosen. The weight (utež) \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\) is a function whose input is a point of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and whose output is a number that is not negative, which is continuous on every outer face of the part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), zero outside \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\), and whose integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) is positive. The force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the load without a body force with the traction vector

\[\bar{\vek t} = \frac{F_{\mathrm{j}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}}{\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}A}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} \tag{4.93}\]

on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Let a solution for a load exist for every such force, with small strains when the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) is small enough. The displacement of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) for a displacement field \(\vek u\) is the number

\[\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \frac{\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek u\,\mathrm{d}A}{\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A} . \tag{4.94}\]

The flexibility coefficient \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the displacement \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) of the solution with small strains for the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\), divided by \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\). The matrix \(\mat D\) with \(m\) rows and \(m\) columns and the elements \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the flexibility matrix of the chosen patches, weights and directions.

Source: EP §4.6.5 (p. 230) and CM §7.4.3 (PDF p. 320), where the two displacements are due to unit forces at points, BARBER (1.18) (PDF p. 27), where the coefficients are called influence coefficients. Patches with weights instead of points are not from the sources.

Does such a weight exist at all? On a patch that is a rectangle on a flat face of the body we build it from two bumps, as in lemma 4.123 we built a bump in a box from three.

Lemma 4.140 Weight on a rectangular patch (utež na pravokotni ploskvici)

Let an outer face of a body be a rectangle in the plane \(z = c\), as for a body made of boxes (definition 4.11, item 2), and let it contain the rectangle \(\Delta S\) of the points \((x, y, c)\) with \(\alpha_1 \le x \le \beta_1\) and \(\alpha_2 \le y \le \beta_2\), where \(\alpha_1 < \beta_1\) and \(\alpha_2 < \beta_2\). Let \(\ell_1 = \beta_1 - \alpha_1\) and \(\ell_2 = \beta_2 - \alpha_2\), let \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) be the bump of lemma 4.123, and at every point of the face let

\[\varphi(x, y, c) = \frac{q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)}{(\ell_1/2)^8\,(\ell_2/2)^8} . \tag{4.95}\]

Then \(\varphi\) is continuous on the face and nowhere negative, it is zero on the edges of \(\Delta S\) and outside it, positive in the interior of \(\Delta S\), equal to \(1\) at the centre of \(\Delta S\), and its integral over the face is

\[\int \varphi\,\mathrm{d}A = \frac{2^{16}}{630^2}\,\ell_1\,\ell_2 = 0{,}1651\,\ell_1\,\ell_2 .\]

The same holds for a face in the plane \(x = c\) or \(y = c\), with the two coordinates that vary on it. If the face belongs to \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), then \(\varphi\), set to zero on the other outer faces of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), is a weight of the patch \(\Delta S\) as in definition 4.139.

Proof

We have to show the continuity, the sign, the value at the centre and the integral, and then that \(\varphi\) is a weight of the definition. Everything follows from the properties of a single bump.

  1. Continuity. By lemma 4.123, item 1, \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) is differentiable at every number, so it is continuous (lemma 1.80). The factor \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\) is therefore a continuous function of the point of the face: for a point \(P_0\) with the coordinate \(x_0\) and an error \(\eta\), the band that the continuity of \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}\) gives at the number \(x_0\) will do, because a difference of coordinates is not larger than the distance between the points, as in step 2 of item 2 of the proof of lemma 4.123. The same holds for the other factor. A product of continuous functions of a point and a multiple of it are continuous (corollary 1.70, item 1).
  2. The sign. The factors \((t - \alpha)^4\) and \((\beta - t)^4\) are powers with an even exponent, so \(q_{\alpha\beta}\) is nowhere negative, and neither is \(\varphi\). If a point lies on the edge of \(\Delta S\) or outside it, then \(x \le \alpha_1\) or \(x \ge \beta_1\) or \(y \le \alpha_2\) or \(y \ge \beta_2\), and the corresponding factor is zero by the definition of the bump. In the interior of \(\Delta S\) both factors are products of positive numbers, so \(\varphi > 0\).
  3. The centre. At \(x = (\alpha_1 + \beta_1)/2\) the numbers \(x - \alpha_1\) and \(\beta_1 - x\) both equal \(\ell_1/2\), so \(q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x) = (\ell_1/2)^8\). The same holds for \(y\), and \(\varphi = 1\).
  4. The integral over the face. By assumption the face is a rectangle that contains \(\Delta S\). The lines \(x = \alpha_1\), \(x = \beta_1\), \(y = \alpha_2\) and \(y = \beta_2\) cut it into at most nine rectangles. On all of them except \(\Delta S\) we have \(\varphi = 0\) by step 2, so by additivity and by the rule for a constant function (lemma 4.10, items 3 and 2, for a rectangle) the integral over the face equals the integral over \(\Delta S\).
  5. By the definition of the integral over a rectangle 4.8 and the linearity of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.54, item 1), with which we take out constant numbers,
    \[\int_{\Delta \mathrm{S}} \varphi\,\mathrm{d}A = \frac{1}{(\ell_1/2)^8\,(\ell_2/2)^8} \int_{\alpha_1}^{\beta_1} q_{\alpha_1\beta_1}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \int_{\alpha_2}^{\beta_2} q_{\alpha_2\beta_2}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  6. The integral of one bump is \(\int_\alpha^\beta (t - \alpha)^4\,(\beta - t)^4\,\mathrm{d}t = \ell^9/630\), where \(\ell = \beta - \alpha\). With SymPy we found a polynomial whose derivative is the integrand, and used the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 1. We insert this into step 5 and get \(\int \varphi\,\mathrm{d}A = (\ell_1^9/630)(\ell_2^9/630)/\big((\ell_1/2)^8\,(\ell_2/2)^8\big) = 2^{16}\,\ell_1\,\ell_2/630^2\).
  7. A weight of the definition. Let the face belong to \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) and let \(\varphi\) be zero on the other outer faces of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). On our face \(\varphi\) is continuous by step 1, on the others it is constantly zero, so it is continuous on every outer face of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). By step 2 it is nowhere negative and zero outside \(\Delta S\). The integral over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the sum of the integrals over the outer faces of \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) (definition 4.11, item 3). These are zero by the rule for a constant function, except the integral over our face, which by steps 4 to 6 equals \(0{,}1651\,\ell_1\,\ell_2 > 0\).

Source: The lemma is not from the sources.

For a patch of \(10\ \text{mm} \times 10\ \text{mm}\) the integral of the weight is \(0{,}1651 \cdot 100\ \text{mm}^2 = 16{,}51\ \text{mm}^2\). A force of 1 kN spread with the weight therefore has the traction vector \(1000\ \text{N}/16{,}51\ \text{mm}^2 = 60{,}56\) MPa at the centre of the patch, while spread evenly it has \(1000\ \text{N}/100\ \text{mm}^2 = 10\) MPa everywhere. The weight gathers the force towards the centre, because the force it loses at the edge, where it falls continuously to zero, it must gain in the middle. By how much? By step 6 of the lemma, one bump on an interval of length \(\ell\) has the average \((\ell^9/630)/\ell = \ell^8/630\), and its largest value is \((\ell/2)^8 = \ell^8/256\) in the middle. Its average is therefore \(256/630 = 0{,}406\) of its largest value. A rectangle of this height has the same area as the bump, since the average is the area under the bump divided by the length of the interval. What the bump loses at the edges, where it is below the rectangle, it therefore gains in the middle, where it is above it.

The weight made of two bumps we average in two steps, as in step 5 of the lemma, where the integral over the rectangle is the product of two integrals. On every line with a constant \(y\) the weight is one bump in \(x\) times a constant number, so its average over this line is \(0{,}406\) of the value in the middle of the line. On the line through the centre this is \(0{,}406\). The average over the whole patch is therefore \(0{,}406\) times the average of the values in the middles of the lines. These values form a bump in \(y\) with the largest value \(1\), so their average is again \(0{,}406\), and the average over the patch is \(0{,}406^2 = 0{,}1651\) of the value \(1\) at the centre. The average traction vector is the same for both spreadings, 10 MPa, because both carry 1 kN on 100 mm². The traction vector at the centre is therefore \(1/0{,}1651 = 6{,}06\) times the even one, as the quotient \(60{,}56\ \text{MPa}/10\ \text{MPa}\) says.

The definition also allows other weights and patches that are not rectangles. It requires continuity on every outer face, no negative values, a positive integral and the existence of a solution. The existence the definition assumes, because we do not prove it in this book. EP remarks that the existence of solutions is difficult to establish, while their uniqueness is easy to prove (EP, p. 225), and we proved the uniqueness in lemma 4.134. The existence, however, is not automatic. Take an edge of the body where the top face with the outward normal \(\vek n_1\) meets the side face with the outward normal \(\vek n_2\), both in \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\). Let the weight on the top face be positive right up to the edge, and let the side face carry no load. By definition 4.133 the stresses of a solution are continuous also on the surface, and Cauchy's formula holds at every point of both faces. Approaching the point \(P\) on the edge along each of the faces, continuity gives at \(P\) \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n_1 = \bar{\vek t}\) and \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n_2 = \vek 0\). Since the stress tensor is symmetric,

\[\vek n_2\cdot\bar{\vek t} = \vek n_2\cdot\ten\sigma\,\vek n_1 = \vek n_1\cdot\ten\sigma\,\vek n_2 = \vek n_1\cdot\vek 0 = 0 .\]

The component of the vector \(\bar{\vek t}\) along \(\vek n_2\) must therefore be zero. If the weight is positive at \(P\) and the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\) has a component along \(\vek n_2\), there is no solution, and the definition gives no coefficient \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) for such a choice. The weight of lemma 4.140 is zero on the edge of the patch, so it is zero on the edge of the body too, and it avoids this problem.

Even with such a weight a solution is not guaranteed. The stresses of a linear elastic solution may grow beyond all bounds at discontinuities of the geometry or of the boundary conditions, for example at the sharp corner of a notch or at a point force, and BARBER reads such solutions as the limit of a corner with a small fillet or of a load over a small part of the surface (BARBER §11.2.1, PDF p. 169). A stress that grows beyond all bounds near a point of the surface is not continuous at that point, so there is no solution of definition 4.133 there. The existence assumption is therefore an assumption about the model. In a real body, which has no sharp corners, the stresses stay finite, while for a body made of boxes with sharp corners the assumption may fail.

The displacement \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the average of the component of the displacement in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\) over the patch, weighted with the weight \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\). If this component equals the same number \(a\) over the whole patch, then by (4.94) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = a \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A/\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A = a\), as it must be for an average. The total force of the load (4.93), the integral of the traction vector over \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), is \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}A/\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}A = F_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\). By lemma 4.134 on the uniqueness of the solution, item 2, the solution with small strains is unique, because the supports prevent every small rigid displacement of the body, so \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a definite number. The name says that \(D_{\mathrm{ij}}\) measures how flexible the body is: how far the patch \(i\) moves per newton of force acting on the patch \(j\). Its unit is metre per newton. For the bracket we need no patches. Force 1 acts at the joint \(C\) horizontally to the right, force 2 at the same joint vertically upwards, along the axis \(y\) and opposite to the load from the start of the chapter. Displacement 1 is the displacement of the joint to the right, displacement 2 the upward one, like \(u\) and \(v\) in (4.88). The matrix

\[\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} D_{\mathrm{xx}} & D_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ D_{\mathrm{yx}} & D_{\mathrm{yy}} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1\ \text{m}}{EA}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 16/3 \\ 16/3 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\]

is the flexibility matrix of the bracket for these two forces. The same patch or the same joint may appear several times, with different directions, as here. The quotient depends only on the patches, weights and directions, not on the magnitude of the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\). For another sufficiently small force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}'\) the solution is, by the principle of superposition and the uniqueness of the solution, \((F_{\mathrm{j}}'/F_{\mathrm{j}})\) times the solution for the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the average \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is linear in the field \(\vek u\), since the integral of a sum splits into the sum of the integrals. For the same reason the displacement under several forces at once is the sum of the contributions,

\[\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{m} D_{\mathrm{ij}}\,F_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad \text{that is} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} \Delta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \Delta_{\mathrm{m}} \end{bmatrix} = \mat D \begin{bmatrix} F_1 \\ \vdots \\ F_{\mathrm{m}} \end{bmatrix} ,\]

where on the right is the product of a matrix and a vector (definition 1.97). For the bracket this is exactly (4.88).

Theorem 4.141 Maxwell's reciprocal theorem (Maxwellov izrek)

Let the body be as in definition 4.133, of an ideal elastic material, and let \(\mat D\) be the flexibility matrix of the chosen patches \(\Delta S_1, \dots, \Delta S_{\mathrm{m}}\), weights \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{\mathrm{m}}\) and directions \(\vek d_1, \dots, \vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\). Then \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = D_{\mathrm{ji}}\) for all \(i\) and \(j\) from \(1\) to \(m\): the flexibility matrix is symmetric.

Proof

We must show that the displacement of the patch \(i\) due to a force of 1 N on the patch \(j\) equals the displacement of the patch \(j\) due to a force of 1 N on the patch \(i\). This is Betti's theorem for two loads that are single forces.

  1. Let \(\vek u^{(1)}\) be the solution with small strains for the force \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) N on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\vek u^{(2)}\) the solution with small strains for the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) N on the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\). When a force of 1 N is not small enough for this, we take a small enough force instead of 1 N in all steps, and the proof stays the same. By definition 4.139 the displacement of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the field \(\vek u^{(2)}\) equals \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} \cdot 1\) N, and the displacement of the patch \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{j}}\) for the field \(\vek u^{(1)}\) equals \(D_{\mathrm{ji}} \cdot 1\) N.
  2. The first load has no body force, and by (4.93) its traction vector on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) is \((1\ \text{N})\,\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}/\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A\). The left side of equation (4.92) is therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \frac{(1\ \text{N})\,\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A = 1\ \text{N} \cdot \frac{\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek u^{(2)}\,\mathrm{d}A}{\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}A} = 1\ \text{N} \cdot D_{\mathrm{ij}} \cdot 1\ \text{N} ,\]
    where we took the constant number out of the integral by the linearity of the integral over the surface, and then used (4.94) and step 1.
  3. In the same way the right side of equation (4.92) equals \(1\ \text{N} \cdot D_{\mathrm{ji}} \cdot 1\ \text{N}\).
  4. By Betti's theorem 4.138 the two sides are equal, so \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = D_{\mathrm{ji}}\).

Source: EP §4.6.5, (4.6.28) (p. 230), CM §7.4.3, (7.4.19), (7.4.20) (PDF p. 320). The sources take the two forces at two different points. The proof does not need this, so the theorem holds also for the same point and two directions, as for the bracket. Forces spread with weights are not from the sources.

The proof showed why the force and the displacement use the same weight. The work of the load \(i\) on the displacements \(\vek u^{(2)}\) is the integral of the weight times the displacement, and exactly this integral, divided by the integral of the weight, is the displacement \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\). With a different weight for the displacement the work would not be the force times the displacement, and Betti's theorem would not give the equality of the coefficients.

For the bracket we saw the symmetry of the flexibility matrix in the computation and proved it in subsection 4.8.4 with the principle of virtual displacements for the truss. For a truss, however, the symmetry is also visible in a formula. Let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{b}}\) be the directions of two forces at the joint \(C\). Let \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(a)}\) be the axial forces in the bars due to a force of 1 N in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\), divided by 1 N, as in the unit dummy load method (theorem 4.96), and likewise \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(b)}\) for the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{b}}\). Under an actual force of 1 N in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{b}}\) the axial force of the bar \(k\) is \(\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(b)} \cdot 1\) N. The unit dummy load method with a unit force in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) gives the component of the displacement in the direction \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\), and dividing it by 1 N we get

\[D_{\mathrm{ab}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(a)}\,\hat N_{\mathrm{k}}^{(b)}\,\frac{L_{\mathrm{k}}}{E_{\mathrm{k}} A_{\mathrm{k}}} .\]

Here \(m\) is the number of bars, as in theorem 4.96, not the number of patches of definition 4.139. Exchanging \(a\) and \(b\) does not change the formula. For our bracket, \(\hat N^{(x)}_{\mathrm{AC}} = 1\) and \(\hat N^{(x)}_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0\) for the horizontal force, and \(\hat N^{(y)}_{\mathrm{AC}} = \tfrac43\) and \(\hat N^{(y)}_{\mathrm{BC}} = -\tfrac53\) for the vertical force upwards (step 2), so \(D_{\mathrm{xy}} = 1 \cdot \tfrac43 \cdot 4\ \text{m}/(EA) + 0 \cdot \big({-\tfrac53}\big) \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = \tfrac{16}{3}\ \text{m}/(EA)\), as in (4.88).

Now we also see why the factor \(\tfrac43\) appeared twice in subsection 4.8.1. The same unit vectors \(\vek n_{\mathrm{AC}}\) and \(\vek n_{\mathrm{BC}}\) tell, in the equilibrium of the pin, how the forces in the bars make up the force on the pin (step 1), and, in the elongations, how the displacement of the pin changes the lengths of the bars (step 4). This connection between equilibrium and geometry is expressed by the principle of virtual displacements for the truss, which we obtained precisely by taking the scalar product of the equilibrium of the pin with the displacement of the pin (section 4.4.9).

For the bracket both forces were at the same joint. Let us also look at two forces at different points (figure 4.436). Take again the steel bar of length 10 m with the cross section \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), held at its top cross section, in the bar model, and this time leave out its weight. By the principle of superposition the displacement due to the weight is simply added to the displacements we compute. The product of Young's modulus and the cross-sectional area is \(EA = 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 78{,}54 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N. Force 1 acts downwards on the cross section at the depth \(x_1 = 5\) m, force 2 downwards at the lower end, at the depth \(x_2 = 10\) m.

  1. A force \(F_1 = 1\) kN at the depth 5 m. The upper half of the bar carries 1 kN and gets longer by \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 324{,}8\) µm. The lower half carries nothing, does not get longer and only moves together with the middle cross section. The lower end therefore moves by 324,8 µm, and \(D_{21} = 324{,}8\) µm/kN.
  2. A force \(F_2 = 1\) kN at the lower end. The whole bar carries 1 kN. The middle cross section moves by the elongation of the upper half, again \(1\ \text{kN} \cdot 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 324{,}8\) µm, and \(D_{12} = 324{,}8\) µm/kN.

Here the mechanism is visible. In both cases the displacement of the other point is the elongation of the part of the bar above the higher of the two points, which carries 1 kN in both cases. In general, for forces at the depths \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) the flexibility coefficient is \(D_{\mathrm{ij}} = \min(x_{\mathrm{i}}, x_{\mathrm{j}})/(EA)\), where \(\min(x_{\mathrm{i}}, x_{\mathrm{j}})\) is the smaller of the two numbers, and exchanging \(i\) and \(j\) does not change it. For the same point \(D_{11} = 5\ \text{m}/(EA) = 324{,}8\) µm/kN and \(D_{22} = 10\ \text{m}/(EA) = 649{,}6\) µm/kN, so

\[\mat D = \begin{bmatrix} 324{,}8 & 324{,}8 \\ 324{,}8 & 649{,}6 \end{bmatrix} \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} .\]

That \(D_{11} = D_{12}\) is a peculiarity of the bar: the middle cross section moves by the elongation of the upper half, which carries 1 kN, no matter where below the middle the force acts.

Let us also test the theorem with two forces spread with weights, on the same bar, held at its top cross section, in the bar model (figure 4.437). The bar has no patches, but a force can be spread over part of its length as a distributed axial load (definition 4.74). Let force 1 be spread between the depths 3 m and 7 m with the weight \((x - 3)^4\,(7 - x)^4\), and force 2 between the depths 5 m and 10 m with the weight \((x - 5)^4\,(10 - x)^4\), depths in metres. Both weights are bumps of lemma 4.123, and we spread the forces as in (4.93), only with an integral over the length instead of over the surface. The displacement \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the average of the displacement \(u(x)\), weighted with the weight of force \(i\). The two loads overlap between 5 m and 7 m. With SymPy we computed for each force of 1 kN the axial force, the displacement and the two averages, and got

\[D_{12} = D_{21} = \frac{4{,}9993\ \text{m}}{EA} = 324{,}76\ \frac{\text{µm}}{\text{kN}} .\]

Why is the number just below \(5\) m? For a point force 1 at the depth \(x\) and a point force 2 at the depth \(x'\) the flexibility coefficient is \(\min(x, x')/(EA)\). With SymPy we checked that for the spread forces \(D_{12}\) is the average of this number, weighted with both weights at once, and such an average does not change when the two weights are swapped. The average depth of force 1 is 5 m, that of force 2 is 7,5 m.

Every pair of points is one point of the rectangle, horizontally at the depth \(x\) of the point of force 1, vertically at the depth \(x'\) of the point of force 2. The diagonal \(x' = x\) separates two cases. On one side \(x' \ge x\) and \(\min(x, x') = x\), the depth of the point of force 1. In the triangle between 5 m and 7 m \(x' < x\), the point of force 2 lies above the point of force 1, and \(\min(x, x') = x'\) is smaller than \(x\) by \(x - x'\). The average of the number \(\min(x, x')\) is therefore smaller than the average depth of force 1, 5 m, by the average of the difference \(x - x'\) over the triangle. In the triangle \(x' < x\), while between 5 m and 7 m the weight of force 2 grows and the weight of force 1 falls. The product of the weights at a point of the triangle is therefore not larger than at the point of the diagonal with the same depth \(x\), where both points are at the same depth between 5 m and 7 m, and there one weight is just rising from zero while the other falls towards zero: the product is everywhere in the triangle below 6 % of its largest value. With SymPy we found that the triangle carries only 0,32 % of the combined weight, and the difference \(x - x'\) in it is 0,22 m on average. That is why \(D_{12}\,EA\) is smaller than 5 m only by \(0{,}0032 \cdot 0{,}22\ \text{m} = 0{,}0007\) m.

What is the theorem good for in measurement? Take a light footbridge with three marked points \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) on the walking surface, and suppose that the bridge behaves linearly elastically (figure 4.439). A point is here a short name for a small patch around it: the load is spread over it with a weight as in definition 4.139, and its displacement is the weighted mean of the displacements of the patch. We load the bridge with a test load of 10 kN at the point \(B\) and measure the vertical displacements downwards: 2,8 mm at \(A\), 5,0 mm at \(B\) and 4,0 mm at \(C\). The numbers are made up for the example. A gauge measures the displacement of its plate, not the weighted mean, but the difference is too small to measure. The point \(A\) is 2,25 m from the left support, and the walking surface goes down by 2,8 mm up to it, on average by 1,2 mm per metre. Even if it is twice as steep at the support, the displacement changes over a plate 10 mm wide by at most \(2{,}5\ \text{mm/m} \cdot 0{,}01\ \text{m} = 0{,}025\) mm. This is less than half of the last measured digit, 0,1 mm, so every average over the plate gives the same measured number. For a plate 10 cm wide, however, the difference would reach 0,25 mm and we would measure it. With the measured displacements we know the column \(B\) of the flexibility matrix, the displacements of all three points per kilonewton of force at \(B\): \(D_{\mathrm{AB}} = 0{,}28\) mm/kN, \(D_{\mathrm{BB}} = 0{,}50\) mm/kN and \(D_{\mathrm{CB}} = 0{,}40\) mm/kN. By Maxwell's theorem we thereby also know the row \(B\): \(D_{\mathrm{BA}} = D_{\mathrm{AB}} = 0{,}28\) mm/kN and \(D_{\mathrm{BC}} = D_{\mathrm{CB}} = 0{,}40\) mm/kN. How far does the point \(B\) go down when 6 kN stand at \(A\) and 4 kN at \(C\)? By adding loads

\[\begin{aligned} \Delta_{\mathrm{B}} &= D_{\mathrm{BA}} \cdot 6\ \text{kN} + D_{\mathrm{BC}} \cdot 4\ \text{kN} = 0{,}28 \cdot 6\ \text{mm} + 0{,}40 \cdot 4\ \text{mm} \\ &= 1{,}68\ \text{mm} + 1{,}60\ \text{mm} = 3{,}28\ \text{mm} . \end{aligned}\]

Without the theorem we would need two tests, with the load at \(A\) and with the load at \(C\), and would measure the displacement at \(B\) each time. With the theorem one test with the load at \(B\) is enough. EP and CM give such an example (EP example 4.6.7, p. 231, CM example 7.4.4, PDF pp. 319-320). If we measured the displacement at many points, one test with the load at \(B\) would tell how far \(B\) goes down when the load stands at any one of them.

The flexibility matrix gives displacements from forces. The reverse, forces from displacements, is given by the stiffness matrix of the bracket, which we obtained in section 4.6.7 from the derivatives of the strain energy with respect to the displacements. It is the inverse matrix of the flexibility matrix (definition 1.110). For the bracket, where \(EA = 1{,}96 \cdot 10^7\) N, we checked with SymPy that

\[\begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix} 10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} \cdot \frac{1\ \text{m}}{EA}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 16/3 \\ 16/3 & 21 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The stiffness matrix is symmetric too. In section 4.6.7 we saw this from the equality of the mixed derivatives of the energy, and COOK proves the symmetry of the stiffness matrix precisely with Betti's theorem (COOK (2.6-1)-(2.6-3), PDF p. 51). The stiffness matrix is the basis of the finite element method, which we will meet in chapter 7.

With this we have reached the end of the chapter. We started with the work of a force and the energy a bar stores. Then we wrote equilibrium as the equality of the work of the external forces and the work of the stresses for every admissible virtual displacement, derived from this form the principle of minimum total potential energy, and with the roles of forces and displacements exchanged the principle of virtual forces. In this section we obtained from the same principle of virtual displacements, used twice, and from the symmetry of the elastic constants that the roles of two loads may be exchanged. The principles of virtual displacements and virtual forces hold for small displacements and any material, since they use only equilibrium and geometry (EP, p. 232). The results that use the strain energy or Hooke's law, from the energy of a bar to the theorems of Betti and Maxwell, also need a linear elastic material that returns the work it receives.
